ber...@mich.com wrote:
> [... snip ...]

> Not that NCL is without it's problems. Personally, I think many of
> the gripes I have with NCL would be dispelled with some simple rules
> changes*:
>
> *Action Modifiers: Minions may not play duplicates of a given card
> during a given action.

This is, and has always been, part of the official rules.

A minion cannot play a second copy of the same action modifier
on a given action.

Also, a minion cannot play a second copy of the same reaction
card on a given action.

> *Combat Cards: Minions may not play duplicates of a given card during
> each round of combat.

This sort of rule has been examined.
It doesn't hold water when one looks at multiple strikes (e.g., you
*should* definately be able to play two Undead Strengths in a round
if you have two strikes.)
And it probably shouldn't apply to damage prevention effects,
either (multiple use of which was an explicit consideration of
the original design, as can be seen in the card text on Sideslip).

It may also unnecessarily restrict Fists of Death, although that
point is an extremely minor one.

> The effect of these would be much like the following examples:
>
> Action Modifiers: After playing a Lost in Crowds, I need more stealth
> to continue my action. Due to the above rule, I can play another
> stealth card but it cannot be another Lost In Crowds.

This is how things work officially, as well.

> Combat Cards: By the above rule it will prevent combat decks from
> emptying their hand for no good reason other than card cycling. At
> Origins I saw folks dropping 2-3 Torn Signposts during a round of
> combat simply because they can. Note: Playing multiple signposts have
> no cumulative effect.

This is a good objective, but a suitable implementation is hard
to come by (things get a bit complicated when you try to word the
rule to allow multiple strikes and damage prevention effects
while disallowing multiple Torn Signposts, etc.)

> The above examples create a Soft Card Limit of sorts, as people
> building a combat deck that want maneuvers would add additional cards
> besides Flash. I also think it falls in line with the No Repeat
> Action, and New Voting rules.

NRA is definately an after-thought rule. It doesn't "feel"
particularly clean and it causes a few complications of its
own (i.e. can a Possessed vampire repeat an action it took
in its previous life? (Yes). or can a minion whose action was
Masked attempt the same type of action? (Yes). and so on.)
Which is why it was left as a DCI rule and not incorporated
into the rulebook proper.

> I kind of clump all of the above into what I term "The One Card Rule".
> All pretty much based on the same principle and promotes more of that
> Game Balance that I keep hearing so much about..

But extending this style of rule to strikes and damage prevention
promotes imbalance, I believe.

> * Vampires are Unique:
> Another thought I've been toying with is that Vampires should be
> unique. That's why they contest when more than 1 are in play at a
> given time. When a given Vampire is Burned or Removed from the Game,
> further copies of that Vampire may no longer be brought into play.
>
> This solves some of the Weenie Madness, and brings Jyhad in line with
> other current game technologies (L5R/DoomTown).
>
> It's a fairly radical thought, but one that makes a lot of sense IMHO.
> Not that it's without problems. Someone like Jimmy Dunn would fall
> under Rule 1.4 which states text on card takes precedence over the
> rulebook.

This idea, suggested a few months (years?) ago by David Pontes, was
also examined. It has its problems, as you note. Those problems
proved too complicated (or too dependent on VtM knowledge) to be
really workable, as well. e.g., a vampire who is retrieved and
then removed by Illusions of Kindred should *not* be restricted
from coming out later (or remaining out, for that matter).

> So before people start beating up on Card Limits, take the above into
> consideration. For a game that was designed by WOTC to be played in a
> NCL environment, Jyhad has stood the test of time pretty well
> considering the lackedasial attitude of it's creators.

Good suggestions. And highly commendable objectives.
But these avenues have been looked into before. So far, a
suitable (simple, effective, and not overly-restrictive)
implementation has been elusive.

Messages.Author: mboh...@shout.net
Messages.Body:
In article <36a81ca2...@news.mich.com>,
ber...@mich.com wrote:

> Not that NCL is without it's problems. Personally, I think many of
> the gripes I have with NCL would be dispelled with some simple rules
> changes*:
>

> *Action Modifiers: Minions may not play duplicates of a given card
> during a given action.

This is in the rules. I'm not sure that it was in the Jyhad rulebook, but
it was definitely in the V:tES rulebook.

> *Combat Cards: Minions may not play duplicates of a given card during
> each round of combat.

In my opinion, this would have other adverse effects that would not make
it worthwhile.

Example A: You're playing Celerity, and your opponent is also playing
Celerity. You have a bad hand or whatever including 2 Sideslips and a Blur.
Your opponent plays a Torn Signpost and will Blur with it. Why shouldn't
you be able to play both Sideslips to dodge his strikes?

Example B: Someone hits you with 8 points of damage, and you don't have
a Skin of Steel in your hand. Why shouldn't you be able to play 2 Skins of
Rock?

> Combat Cards: By the above rule it will prevent combat decks from
> emptying their hand for no good reason other than card cycling. At
> Origins I saw folks dropping 2-3 Torn Signposts during a round of
> combat simply because they can. Note: Playing multiple signposts have
> no cumulative effect.

If someone dropped 2-3 Torn Signposts, I wouldn't be worried about it.
It has several things of interest attached to it. First, he just wasted
1 or 2 Torn Signposts. Second, he may be panicking because he doesn't have
cards in his hand that he wants. Third, his deck is probably poorly
constructed. These last two points help you out.

There are very few instances where multiples of combat cards throw things
out of whack to begin with, IMO. These would be Increased Strength,
Fists of Death, Weather Control, and superior Terror Frenzy. Most other
cards that would be powerful in multiples have card text restricting them
like Carrion Crows or have costs that make multiples inefficient.

> The above examples create a Soft Card Limit of sorts, as people
> building a combat deck that want maneuvers would add additional cards
> besides Flash.

Forcing people to use different cards simply for the sake of doing so is
not a good thing, IMO. Plus, you still can't maneuver to cancel your own
maneuver. And by removing some Flash, you are forced to substitue other
press cards if you want to press. Putting in lots of Flash can already
have its own adverse effects - DotB causes hand jam as does just having
multiples in your hand at once.

> I also think it falls in line with the No Repeat Action, and New Voting
> rules.

I'm not sure how this associates to NRA, as S:CE and untap without NRA
is nuts... I'm still trying to convince my group of that, but apparently
they don't mind always losing to the weenie Protean Computer Hacking hordes
when I decide to play that deck.

The vote pushing rules are different than combat card dumping. First, you
can dump the vote cards during any political action. It doesn't even have
to be yours. And when you have weenies, you're eventually going to get a
vote action through to dump them. The cards serve three purposes - calling
the vote, passing the vote, and getting perhaps more useful cards into your
hand. With combat, if you are dumping cards, you may more may not be
moving towards accomplishing your goal - putting vampires in torpor or burning
them. For example, playing 3 Torn Signposts does you no good. A more
proper equivalent to VP would be playing 3 Fists of Death, but you've also
just spent 3 blood and aren't assured of actually being able to hit your
target.

> * Vampires are Unique:
> Another thought I've been toying with is that Vampires should be
> unique. That's why they contest when more than 1 are in play at a
> given time. When a given Vampire is Burned or Removed from the Game,
> further copies of that Vampire may no longer be brought into play.

This is essentially a card limit on the crypt. The reason being, if
a core vampire of yours gets burned for whatever reason, you had better
have replacements. This would possibly help combat decks and hurt weenie
decks, but I'm not sure that it'd be sufficient to counteract all the other
effects.

> This solves some of the Weenie Madness, and brings Jyhad in line with
> other current game technologies (L5R/DoomTown).

Jyhad is not L5R or DoomTown. We will not be assimilated. :)

> It's a fairly radical thought, but one that makes a lot of sense IMHO.
> Not that it's without problems. Someone like Jimmy Dunn would fall
> under Rule 1.4 which states text on card takes precedence over the
> rulebook.

Jimmy's powerful enough already, but his card text actually becomes about
even between benefit and penalty depending on whether anyone else is playing
with him.

> So before people start beating up on Card Limits, take the above into
> consideration. For a game that was designed by WOTC to be played in a
> NCL environment, Jyhad has stood the test of time pretty well
> considering the lackedasial attitude of it's creators.

The limit on reaction and action modifiers makes sense, especially the one
on action modifiers, because of the effects of multiples. S&B is pretty
strong when not faced by heavy bounce or determined rush. But just imagine
if it only had to use Lost in Crowds to stack up the stealth it needed?
The same goes for vote push. Combat cards, for the most part, either
aren't stackable or aren't worth playing multiples of. The vampire thing
makes for an interesting house rule, but there's no real big use for it
other than a slight curtailment of weenie decks.

Mike

Mike Bohlmann, MAIP - Prince of Urbana-Champaign
http://www.shout.net/~mbohlman/

When facing a bleed deck you don't know he has Conditioning???

The fun is in the strategy of deck design vs deck design and of building decks.
Personally, I enjoy Jyhad because it is a deeply rich strategy game with
almost infinite possibility. Part of this enjoyment comes from other players
in a particular game trying their darndest to kill me, through clever game play
and clever deck design. I don't, however, play Jyhad because I get a great joy
out of being surprised by what card my opponent turns over next (well, unless
it is particularly funny...). If my opponent has a well designed,
strategically effective deck that happens to contain 30 of one particular card,
who am I to say he shouldn't. I have seen all the cards. I know what they all
look like. My enjoyment of the game is not increased because on this action my
opponent played a Conditioning where as last action my opponent played a
Threats. I'm not playing the game to see different cards. I'm playing for the
strategy that comes from pitting good decks against good decks.

"This my good man is a load of crap. I could respond in the same vein

with NL is a crutch for poor playing skill. I mean I could train a monkey
mindlessly pump out Bums Rush, IG, Torn Signpost, and Undead Strength on every
vampire in play."

But you couldn't train said clever monkey A) how to build an effective one or
B) how to win with such a deck.

"That is not a deck it's a combo. A deck is a group of multiple combo's that
all work together to form a stratagy."

Whatever makes you happy.

"A lot of the "deck's" I see posted are the same 4 or 5 cards repeted
endlessly. It takes much more deck building skill with a limit than without,
and more playing skill to win with a 4CL deck.Rather than endlessly repeating
the same combo over and over and over....."

Ok. Before this thread continues, please, I repeat, please go to Mark
Langsdorf's Jyhad web page (search for Langsdorf+Jyhad. It'll show up easily.
Go on. Go there. Right now.) You will find many articles regarding this
subject. Many pro Card Limit essays. Many anti-card limit essays. Read them
all. You will see how the argument you stated in the above post has be
presented (many, many times, I might add) and systematically refuted on every
possible point. Over and over again. Please. Go now.

"I just love arguing about this"

Then you really should get better at it.

Mind you, the argument between various persons on this group and Noal regarding
CL is a different argument than you have presented here. Noal is claiming that
his particular play group likes playing 6CL because he feels that it increases
the variatey of the decks that show up at the table. People disagree with the
idea that a CL increases variety (I know I do...), but no one has a beef with
Noal 'cause he likes to play this way. My main arguing point with Noal was
over his statement that no deck suffered from a 6CL environement, which I feel
is completely incorrect. He is not, however, neccessarily stating that a
blanket CL is good for the game as a whole, so I suspect you won't get any
support there.

No, they're not wasted card positions. They're included to lean the
laws of probability in your favor to assure that you always have the
card, since you will always need the card. For example, skill cards.
I play a deck that has a crypt of 12 4-cap vampires with inferior
Dominate. I have 12 Dominate skill cards in my deck. I only expect
to get six vampires out during any given game. I require superior
Dominate, since I have many Governs in the deck and the idea is to get
a vampire out, give him DOM, and then let him Govern at superior and
get a second vampire out for 1 transfer. Then give HIM DOM, and let
them both Govern at superior and get two more vampires out for 2
transfers. This means I get 4 vampires, two with superior DOM, and
two with inferior, for a total of 7 pool. Now, why do I have 12 cards
and not 6? So that I'm assured of drawing the skill cards EARLY in
the game, instead of LATER, when it will be much too late. I can
always discard the extra skill cards later, but if I have to bring out
four vampires manually and pay 16 pool instead of 7, then the deck has
failed in one of its stated purposes - get vampires out cheap.

Simply put: it's basic probability math. get a calculator and figure
it out.

First of all I Just wanted to say thanks you to LSJ for responding
in a well written manner to my post of thoughts. I'm not a guy that
continuously looks to the rulebook for every little thing, so please
cut me a little slack if I slip occasionally.

One of the things that has always bothered me about
this newsgroup is the focus on how best to manipulate
a loophole. Please don't take that the wrong way, I'm
not out to slam anyone today (though the day ain't over,
>;-)

V:TES is a wonderful game, where I now find myself discovering
new and amusing ways to pound my friends. Having been an
avid player, I can't help but be bothered by some of the card flow
during matches.

Why should people be able to play multiples of a given card during
combat? Why should you be able to play 4 or 5 skins of rock?
How many layers is "Your" epidermous? (Hmm, just remembered
I never took biology).

After playing in the soft 6CL environ for the past year or two, it
would appease many of the problems that I have with the NCL
environment. Fun decks aside, many of the decks I've seen under NCL
are pretty much "no-brainers". Much like the Form of Mist/Bleed combo
mentioned earlier.

One of members of my group commented about multiple strike cards, and
that you should be able to use multiple Undead Strengths (fer
instance). I agree. Pretty easy to expand my original idea to
include the above.

On another note, Mike Bohlman responded about the idea of Vampires
being Unique:

B> * Vampires are Unique:
B> Another thought I've been toying with is that Vampires should be
B> unique. That's why they contest when more than 1 are in play at a
B> given time. When a given Vampire is Burned or Removed from the
B>Game, further copies of that Vampire may no longer be brought into
B>play.

M>This is essentially a card limit on the crypt. The reason being, if
M>a core vampire of yours gets burned for whatever reason, you had
M>better have replacements. This would possibly help combat decks and
M>hurt weenie decks, but I'm not sure that it'd be sufficient to
M>counteract all the other effects.

I disagree. It is not a card limit on the crypt, it is a tool that
will encourage people to spend a bit more forethought on Crypt
construction.

B> This solves some of the Weenie Madness, and brings Jyhad in line
B>with other current game technologies (L5R/DoomTown).

M>Jyhad is not L5R or DoomTown. We will not be assimilated. :)

Can't argue that. Though I am very interested in learning more about
Legend of the Burning Sand. Part of it's game dynamic is supposed to
be very much like Jyhad.

One last comment. V:TES as a game was created on the coattails of
MAGIC way back when. Magic has evolved beyond it's original inception
and other games (like L5R and DT) have set a new standard which should
not be ignored. I'm not a big fan o' change in VTES (I'm sure a few
of ya'll can remember my ranting about 7/7), but a sensible evolution
of the game would be a boon. Of course, no such evolution could occur
unless WOTC were to do another revision of the game to the general
masses.

Thanks for listening.

cgo...@sprynet.com wrote:

[ Yet another pro-CL post with the same points as others snipped ]

> So I ask anyone to show me where a CL does not make you a better player or

Does anyone else notice it besides me that almost every pro-CL post
brings up the same points over and over again as the pro-NL (rather than
anti-CL) counters each point? Yet there is never a new real counter-counter
point to the NL counter points.

Pro-CL arguments:
A) Force you to be more innovative with your deck designs
B) Fix cards that are much more powerful than comparable cards
C) Allow anyone with a small collection to make a deck that competes with
Mr. Suitcase
Are there any other pro-CL arguments that I'm missing?

Pro-NL counter arguments:
A) Actually require less thought because you just put in 4 or 6 or
whatever of each card that does what you need. With a CL, the
ability for knowing whether to use Guard Dogs or Rat's Warning in
your deck falls to the wayside as you just put in the max of each or
the max of one and some of the other.

I've played in many very competitive CL groups including 4CL and 6CL.
It was quite a deckbuilding challenge to convert to NL because it really
is difficult to decide what is enough and what is too much of a given
card. The NL decks containing 15 to 20 copies of a given card that
the pro-CL crowd would like to think make up the majority of NL decks
are far and few between.

B) Short answer: the super powerful cards aren't any less powerful, they
just show up less often. Yes, there are counters to each of the
reworded power cards. However, regular defenses work fine except when
having to deal with these cards; special defense preparations have to
be made. For example, I don't plan on blocking any bleeds because I
have enough deflection and pool gain to keep up with a heavy bleeder.
But then Return to Innocence shows up, and I've already played my 6
Deflections and can't block the bleed.

C) While Mr. Handbag has maybe 8 of a given common and 1 of a comparable
rare, Mr. Suitcase has more of the common card and probably 8 of the
comparable rare. So Mr. Handbag, under a 6CL, uses 6 of the common and his
1 rare. Mr. Suitcase uses 6 of the common, but can also use 6 of his rare.
And Mr. Suitcase is unlikely to give away his two extra rares. Under NL, Mr.
Suitcase could give Mr. Handbag all the copies of the common that he wants
and not be affected by the reduced card pool. So Mr. Suitcase is basicaly
unaffected by a CL.

I'm not against CL if that's what people want to play, but I'll always be
a proponent for NL in my own groups and official tournaments. :)

Mike

When the game was designed, they opted to move away from Rare = Powerful

>you're going to be consistently drawing wasted guns...

Selective snippage, at best... What are your thoughts on the rest of
Derek's post, specifically regarding cost and criteria for evaluating
the expense of Zip Gun/DBR. Are his cirteria valid?
Do you follow the comparisons to other sources of agg. damage, and
their associated costs?
What's the justification for Zip/DBR's real expense being so much less
than comparable effects (if you agree with Derek's applied criteria)?

I feel that we've been well served by the revisions made to cards to
date. I watched from _early_ on in M:t$$ how the introduction of a
4CL had next to zero impact on the outrageous combos/power cards in
the game. Next came a restricted list. Then cards were outright
banned. Still, no effect on the basic way competitive play goes.
(Find the overly powerful combo, and run as many iterations on it as
deck space and card limitations will allow) Its so much better to
alter a card, allowing it to be usable without being
overpowered/undercosted. When balance of effect is applied on a card
by card basis, card limits become moot. Powerful deck ideas then come
from the successful merging of well thought out combinations of cards
plus astute game play. Imposing a card limit on this sort of
environment becomes an interesting artifact or meta-game alteration,
but doesn't improve the game from its original design.

(This paragraph assumes, of course, that you're not doing something
like putting 4 Wakes, 4 Forced Awakenings, and 4 2nd Traditions in
your deck, which is just a complicated way to say "12 untap reaction
cards, and 4 of them are really good if you're a Prince.")

If you're only putting 4 Wakes in the deck, why are you bothering to
Wake since you're, due to not having it in your hand most of the time,
going to have to leave people untapped a lot to block anyway? I don't
know how your playgroup works, but if someone taps out I will -assume-
they are holding a Wake in their hand -- but I will *also* assume that
they're only holding ONE, and so I had better be ready to send two
guys with the same action. I'm not going to hold back my first Govern
for a bleed of 3 just because I think you might have a Wake - i'm
going to do it, let you Wake if you have it, let you fail to replace
the card, then send the NEXT guy to Govern for 3 and see if you had
*two* in your hand, and if you don't, then I'm going to Condition it.
If I don't do this, then I'm taking NO actions and you don't EVER
waste the Wake. If you have Guard Rats or Dog's Warning (sic), I
might consider putting only 4 wakes in since my bleed untap is taken
care of and I only need to stop OTHER things. But then I'm packing
two kinds of untap in my hand and i'm down to 5 cards for when I -do-
untap. Hmm. Messy.

If your deck is designed to intercept people, it already suffers from
the classic "can usually only intercept my predator" problem. The
simplest way to balance out an intercept deck is to let your minions
all take actions and Wake people as necessary to do the intercepting
for your defense or when your prey does something to help himself. 4
Wakes are a joke in this instance - you're going to want to tap out
more often than 4 turns, and if you are facing a Misdirection tap &
bleed deck you'll get pummelled when you run out of Wakes, since he
won't be bothering to waste Misdirections until you leave guys
untapped.

> I prefer 8 or none, myself, to make sure that I'll have it
>> handy when I need it, or to just not bother and remember not to tap
>> everyone - tap & bleeds aren't all -that- common because of all the
>> untap available.
>
>8 or none? I now see the subtlety that NCL allows. It's not all about being
>sure you have, if it is in the minds of your opponents 'Dagmar always has a
>untap card', you have saved deck space and hand jam.

Under 4CL and using 90 card decks, I'm going to assume you DON'T have
it, and i'll be right most of the time. Every time I see one I'll be
happily counting, and when you untap 4 times I won't even bother to do
"tempting" actions first to see if you burn the Wake there. "Wanna
come stop my KRC? It'll hurt you... Aw. you stopped it. OK, well,
this OTHER guy will Fifth Tradition himself ... oops, used your wake?
Shame."

And yes, there is some subtlety involved - if I always have it the
first few times I need it, my opponent has no idea if I've gone hog
wild and put 20 in the deck, or if I've only put 4 in the deck and
just played my last one. Both are perfectly conceivable. (although
i'd reduce that to 12 instead of 20 to avoid having NOTHING but wakes
in my hand.. but that's beside the point.) Especially if I have a
deck that actually packs some punch behind its blocks.

But rest assured, a lot of it is also being sure that YOU have it,
just in case someone decides to say "Nah. You didn't put THAT many
in." and tap out all his guys trying to get you.

>>
>> A 6CL is still much more like a 4CL than an NL, though. 6 wakes mean
>> you either buy Sabbat for Forced Awakening or get raped by tap &
>> bleed. 6 Rush actions mean you either buy Sabbat for Ambush or just
>> don't play combat decks. 6 skill cards mean you can't design crypts
>> with -everyone- at inferior, since you aren't guaranteed more than 1
>> or 2 in the early game. 6 Immortal Grapples mean that S:CE rules
>> supreme in the combat world. There's just too much you can't do under
>> a 6CL that you must have NL in order to do.
>

>Of course some strategies are more viable playing the game with different
>rules. We would not be having this discussion if the games allowed identical
>game play. And so the issue comes down to personal preference for the style
>of play encouraged by the specific rulings.

I do not believe that the designers of the game wished combat to be a
joke. A 4CL or even a 6CL makes combat a joke. When nearly any deck
that wants to can just shrug off a combat deck with minimal effort,
the balance is, well, not balanced.

>In any event S:CE has many more counters than IG, many of them involving
>never getting into combat in the first place. If you are playing Rush and

so what do you do when your prey is an intercept/run-away deck? You
attempt to act. Your prey intercepts you and plays S:CE. You attempt
a second action. Your prey intercepts you and plays S:CE. Your
predator comes to bleed you. You wake and block. He plays Form of
Mist. You could've not got into combat, sure - he would've still bled
you and discarded the Form of Mist at end of turn (since he probably
had 2 after not getting to play any). "not getting into combat" is
not a worthwhile counter to S:CE, as that basically is acquiescing to
the idea that combat wasn't supposed to be in Jyhad anyway, which is
patently false.

>your prey happens to be Captain Defender of course your strategy is going to
>have an uphill struggle, but this is as true in NCL. Don't blame the rules
>for the results of your unfortunate placing; change seating with politics,

Assuming you're playing a vote deck.

>encourage others to waste his S:CE with HAven uncovered and bribes (political

Oh, yes, THAT'll go. "Hey Mr. Rush deck, would you come waste some
Rush actions on my prey with a Haven please? He's got this nasty S:CE
and I just can't do a THING to him when I block him."

>or Succubus Club). If you rely on one [card?] strategy you are often going
>to be crippled -in both enviroments- should other decks [prey-predator
>especially] happen to be effective against you. That's the luck of the draw
>in meta game.

not often... not if you build the deck right. Most decks can, when
properly built, deal with many different predators. IG hoses S:CE
decks. S:CE hoses Gangrel claw decks. Gangrel claw decks hose IG.
Note the well-balanced vicious circle? Make that a 4CL and IG
immediately suffers - 4 IG vs. 4 Majesty + 4 Staredown + 4 Catatonic
Fear vs. 4 Claws of the Dead + 4 Wolf Claws + 4 Bone Spur. And if
that wasn't bad enough, the Gangrel can even S:CE with two different
cards themselves. Under 4CL, the poor IG deck is just going to be

yeah, but there are an awful lot of vampires who have Presence. Or

Giovanni.

Me >Pro-NL counter arguments:
Me > A) Actually require less thought because you just put in 4 or 6 or
Me > whatever of each card that does what you need.

> Putting in 8-12 of the card under NCL is even less mentally taxing. However...

8 to 12. That's a four card swing. Too many and you'll hand jam.
Too few, and you won't have them when you need them. For people that
have never played NL extensively, I know that this can be difficult to
understand, but that's the way it works. Choosing the right amount is
quite difficult until you get good at NL deck construction. And even
then, it takes several games to figure out if you've got the right
amount.

For CL, you might only have one or two options for a card you want as a
backbone to your deck. So you put in the max of the one that matches
exactly what you want (no thought) and possibly the max of the second
card (some to no thought). If there is no comparable card to the
first, there is no thought whatsoever to how many you should put in.

And I'm not speaking in theory, I'm speaking from most of my Jyhad
experience playing under CL, either 4CL or 6CL. I played with CL for
about 3 years. I've only played NL for the last year or so.

> NCLer 'But you just use the second tier cards instead, that not innovative!'
>
> This is a slanted view; of course in many instances second tier
> cards will be employed (which saves them from wallpaper, and is -as-
> creative as putting in 8-12 in the first place).

Ok, as you see above, I use the word "thought." I can accept "less
mentally taxing" as the same as "requiring less thought." And I'll give
you a little leeway with "innovative." But in no way does "thought"
equal "creativity," at least in my book.

"Thought" is trying to decide how many of a given card to put in.
"Creativity" in Jyhad is figuring out some strategy or card that
isn't obvious. For example, Noal's "The Grind" deck is creative.
It does something new that isn't entirely obvious.

> However, in the situation where there is no
> standard second tier card, a 'creative solution' is -demanded-.

Of course. Whereas CL _requires_ creativity to get around the CL,
NL groups push towards creativity. Creativity in CL is a
necessity so that you can get around the CL. However, CL and NL
have the same creativity available when it comes to designing
interesting new deck ideas. The problem with CL is that your
creative deck ideas may be limited by some cards not having second
tier options.

Robert Goudie brought up something a lot of us NL'ers have
forgotten - the transition from CL to NL. At first, a group that
switches to NL will probably see lots of non-creative decks as
they explore the NL strategy. That means heavy S&B decks, decks
composed entirely of a few cards, etc. As the group's NL skills
mature, they will be back to creating competitive, creative decks
that can also stand up to S&B monsters.

> Of course this eliminates several 'pure' strategies, but the idea
> isn't about specific strategies being available, it's about there
> being a derth of strategies available.

Under NL, there are multitudes of deck strategies. Under CL, there
are also many deck strategies available, but those under NL which
have require more of a card that has no second-tier option are right
out.

Me > B) Short answer: the super powerful cards aren't any less powerful,
Me > they just show up less often.

>
> I don't really grasp your counter point... we are restricting all cards,
> because it is considered unbalancing for 'super powerful cards' (your words,
> so you suggest they exist) to appear in greater numbers. Without even
> needing to cite examples your 'rebuttal' is my argument; They do indeed show
> up less often, and hence have less inpmact on the game. So in essence you
> agree that 4CL does lessen the impact of 'imbalanced' cards?

They do not lessen the impact. A Return to Innocence has the
same effect whether it is played under CL or without CL. If a
person isn't prepared for it, they are ousted. This isn't like
a Presence bleed that you can see coming each turn. This isn't
like a Dominate bleed that you can see coming each turn. Any
deck can use it at anytime (well, they need vampires of course:).
The point is, if you aren't prepared for a 10 point bleed, you
are dead. The way you have to prepare for it under CL and NL
is the same. The impact is just the same.

Me > C) While Mr. Handbag has maybe 8 of a given common and 1 of
Me > a comparable rare, Mr. Suitcase has more of the common card
Me > and probably 8 of the comparable rare.

> In your experience that may be the case. We have played 4CL
> almost exclusively. 5 years of trading has seen collections
> evolve to 4s and 4s and 4s. Indeed Mr. Suitcase often has 2-4
> of any given given rare. Mr Handbag [great term by the way]
> often has 2-4 rares -for the decks which were his favourites-.

Hasn't Jyhad only been around since fall 1994? Not significant,
but anyway. What you are saying is that after years of trading
everyone in your group has more or less the cards they want to
make the decks they want under 4CL, correct? Ok, two counter-
points.

First, I thought CL was supposed to increase creativity, but
yet the Mr. Handbags (thanks, btw:) in your group have
traded for rares to go in their favorite decks. Wouldn't that
mean that they've been playing the same decks since you
started? Sure, they might have others, but the ones they play
the most are basically the same as when you started. That
doesn't sound very creative to me.

Second, what happens if a new Mr. Handbag wants to join the
group? They don't have the benefit of years of trading with
you guys and have a lot of catching up to do. It is possible
that the pool is there to get him up to speed quickly, but
what if that pool of rares isn't there?

Note, this shows how CL is perfectly reasonable for home
play, and I have nothing against that. But for tournament
play, this reasoning just won't hold.

> This point boils down to differing play groups, and only serves
> to emphasise that rare cards that are without second tier common
> equivalents will give the edge to Mr Suitcase -in either
> enviroment-, but according to your figures even more so in NCL
> in which trading and purchasing was geared to increasing the
> disparity.

In the Jyhad set, the rare cards were usually second-tier to
commons in general situations, but perhaps better in specialized
situations. When speaking of tiers of cards, NL'ers hold that
commons are the first tier cards as they make up the majority of
a person's deck while the rares (and sometimes uncommons) serve
as second tier. Everyone has equal access to the commons, ie
the first tier cards. There is, however, disparity of the rares.
Under CL, Mr. Handbag is restricted from using the commons that
he has all that he wants, perhaps freely given by Mr. Suitcase.

Mark > D) In your dreams [that CL stops S&B]

>
> Many suggest gentlemanly play, and evolved gamemanship as
> restraining factors in the non-play of degenerate decks.
> Even without needing to cite such a weak, but prominent
> argument common to both sides, the arrival of such cards
> as Protected Resources and Archon Investigation made S&B
> degeneracy much less of a head-ache (whilst admittedly
> conferring a 'must have' cachet on these cards).

Which are rare and uncommon respectively and require
purchasing the more expensive V:tES vs. the cheaper Jyhad.
That doesn't look good for Mr. Handbag.

> The fact remains that we want to win in intriguing and
> 'cool' ways just as much as you do and will similarly try
> new ideas... just try playing pure Ravnos in 4CL with no
> Sabbat. 4CL doesn't tame S&B anymore than NCL does, unless
> of course you are gambling on that counter strategy , and

Under NL, you can be prepared for S&B without a gentlemanly
agreement. That includes bounce, reduce, rush, intercept, and
pool gain. With a CL and especially so with 4CL, your access
to some of these is limited. Take, for example, bounce. You
have Redirection and Deflection with Deflection being preferable
if you have vampires that keep plenty of blood and because
Redirection requires two cards to play after you do it once
(WwEF/FA/untap and Redirection). Obviously, Redirection is
a weak alternative to Deflection when you want your vampires
taking actions and not being untapped. Under NL, you can use
8 Deflections where under 4CL, you use 4 Deflections and 4
Redirections. It's a crapshoot for which you'll have when
you really need a Deflection.

Mark > Thanks, Mike.
Mark > Remember folks, there's a $50 bounty for a literate article
Mark > that rebuts Pro-NL counter arguments A-D without simply
Mark > repeating Pro-CL arguments A-D. Easy money. I'm good for
Mark > it.

> touche?

Not quite. Btw, thanks for the well thought out arguments and counter-
counter points. I look forward to your response. It's nice to have
a CL actually come up with something well thought out that just doesn't
repeat what's already been said.

Mike

Messages.Author: Petri Wessman
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 26 Jan 1999 08:53:16 GMT, lor...@nospam.nineball.org (Derek S. Ray) said:

>> Where did you pull this startling piece of wisdom from? I am no tournament
>> player, but I would suggest that 4,3 2 or even 1 WWEF can be incredibly
>> useful.

Derek> If you're only putting 4 Wakes in the deck, why are you
Derek> bothering to Wake since you're, due to not having it in your
Derek> hand most of the time, going to have to leave people untapped a
Derek> lot to block anyway?

Look up "bluff" in the dictionary :)

Ummm... I really don't see this "must reliably always have Wake in
hand to include it in deck" point. In fact I think it's silly. Yes,
it's a viable deck design to make a deck that virtually always can
Wake, but to claim it's the only useful use for Wakes is tunnel
vision.

I usually put 1-5 Wakes in decks, depending on the deck. For intercept
decks I usually put more, but I've found 1-4 Wakes to be extremely
useful. Why? Because it keeps people on their toes. Once I demonstrate
that I have Wakes, I can use it to bluff, tapping out and letting
people think that I have a Wake when in fact I don't - or doing it
only when I have a Wake, depending on how the game is going. You know,
"mind games" and "strategy"? :) Being predictable is a bad thing.

In short: if you're basing a deck around the concept that it must
always be able to Wake, then using N of them is a good idea. But I
strongly disagree with the idea that that's the *only* way to use
Wakes. Your mileage may vary, of course.

//Petri

CPilhatsch> In article <36a91dab...@news.mich.com>,

>> should preclude Strike:CE. First Strike should at least be able to

CPilhatsch> I agree with you wholeheartedly on this. It *should* be
CPilhatsch> able to beat at least the dodge. *sigh*

AGREED!

As it is, First Strike is a joke. In addition, it's very aggravating
to try to explain to newbies why something called "first strike"
doesn't work like a first strike - it actually resolves *after* S:CE
and dodge. It makes no game world sense, it makes no general sense.

I'd love to see First Strike resolved *first*, then S:CE and Dodge. I
really can't see why it isn't that way, except "that's the way the
Rules Team ruled it once upon a time". Or maybe there is a good
argument, but I haven't heard it yet.

In a game world sense, the current ruling doesn't make sense. First
Strike means a surprise attack, it just doesn't compute that somebody
would be able to use Majesty against that or dodge the attack when
they don't know it's coming. I know, I know, game world rationales
don't wash when it comes to the card game - but I can tell you that
the illogic behind the current rule *does* create problems when
explaining the game, from personal experience.

As is, S:CE is an extremely powerful effect, and something that a lot
of combat clans have great problems with. First Strike isn't a very
common ability, and having it resolve first would give the Assamites a
fighting chance (pun semi-intended :).

LSJ (or others): is there any chance of changing the rules to that
effect? Since the rules have already effectively been changed N times
recently with the ton of errata and stuff, I don't see it as an
impossible thing. Also since the new rules (available as PDF) haven't
been officially printed in any form, there would be no distribution
costs or stuff like that.

In any case, I'd like to hear people's opinions/discussion on this. Am
I in the minority here, or would something like this benefit the game?
Are there things that it could break?

I personally would like it for the following reasons:

a) "It would make sense", and it would be easier and more logical to
explain to beginners.

b) It would give clans with First Strike capability (Assamites at the
forefront) some much-needed boost.

c) It would give one more general way of fighting S:CE. Since S:CE is
(IMHO) an overly powerful effect, this is (again IMHO) a very good
thing.

Negatives:

a) All rule changes are things that should be approached with caution.

b) It might break something or introduce something really broken into
the game. Nothing comes to mind yet, but there might be something
I'm missing. Ok, Assamites might actually become frightening
instead of jokes :)

Opinions?

//Petri

Messages.Body:
Petri Wessman wrote:
> On Tue, 26 Jan 1999 11:22:51 GMT, CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at said:
>> ber...@mich.com wrote:
> >> Thought I'd mention that I've always been a BIG fan that First Strike

>

> CPilhatsch> able to beat at least the dodge. *sigh*
>

>
> As it is, First Strike is a joke. In addition, it's very aggravating
> to try to explain to newbies why something called "first strike"
> doesn't work like a first strike - it actually resolves *after* S:CE
> and dodge. It makes no game world sense, it makes no general sense.

Game World:

To strike, your fist (or other strike element) must traverse the
distance from you to your opponent. When striking with First Strike,
either your traverse that distance faster (e.g., Fast Hands) or
you attack from a position/vantage point that allows your strike
to connect before your opponent can connect his strike to you
(e.g., Back Stab).

When Dodging, however, you are not attempting to get your strike
from here to there. You are simply moving out of the way of the
incoming strike.

When ending combat, the situation is much the same.

> I'd love to see First Strike resolved *first*, then S:CE and Dodge. I
> really can't see why it isn't that way, except "that's the way the
> Rules Team ruled it once upon a time".

Actually, no ruling was ever necessary, since (for Dodge) the rulebook
says very clearly: "[Dodge] negates the effect of the opponent's strike
that round." (Jyhad 15.3)

Some people (prossibly influenced by the MtG notion of "First Strike")
questioned it, so the clarification that, "yes, this is true, even
against First Strke" was issued. (RTR 22-DEC-94)

For S:CE, the rulebook was even clearer (Jyhad 15.3):

[S:CE] ends combat immediately (before any damage is dealt or any
strike's effects take place). Note that combat ends is not affected
by Dodge and even cancels strikes with first strike.

> Or maybe there is a good
> argument, but I haven't heard it yet.

See above.

> In a game world sense, the current ruling doesn't make sense. First
> Strike means a surprise attack, it just doesn't compute that somebody
> would be able to use Majesty against that or dodge the attack when
> they don't know it's coming.

It doesn't mean "surprise attack" (see above).
That's what Hidden Lurker mimics - and Hidden Lurker *does* thwart
dodge and S:CE.

> I know, I know, game world rationales
> don't wash when it comes to the card game - but I can tell you that
> the illogic behind the current rule *does* create problems when
> explaining the game, from personal experience.

Try using "real world" terms that work to convey the official
operation. Certainly using terms like "surprise attack" when
descibing First Strike can lead to confusion.

> As is, S:CE is an extremely powerful effect, and something that a lot
> of combat clans have great problems with. First Strike isn't a very
> common ability, and having it resolve first would give the Assamites a
> fighting chance (pun semi-intended :).

Not that this line of argument is related to how the rules should
operate, Assamites do have access to both Hidden Lurker and Psyche!
for combating S:CE.

> LSJ (or others): is there any chance of changing the rules to that
> effect? Since the rules have already effectively been changed N times
> recently with the ton of errata and stuff, I don't see it as an
> impossible thing. Also since the new rules (available as PDF) haven't
> been officially printed in any form, there would be no distribution
> costs or stuff like that.

Not likely, since it isn't a problem (or, if it is a problem, it isn't
severe enough to warrant such a change).

--

http://www.wizards.com/VTES/VTES_Rules.html

<or...@termiitti.akumiitti.fi> wrote:

>On Tue, 26 Jan 1999 08:53:16 GMT, lor...@nospam.nineball.org (Derek S. Ray) said:
>
>Derek> If you're only putting 4 Wakes in the deck, why are you
>Derek> bothering to Wake since you're, due to not having it in your
>Derek> hand most of the time, going to have to leave people untapped a
>Derek> lot to block anyway?
>
>Look up "bluff" in the dictionary :)

and see "Calling one's" right after it. ;)

>Ummm... I really don't see this "must reliably always have Wake in
>hand to include it in deck" point. In fact I think it's silly. Yes,
>it's a viable deck design to make a deck that virtually always can
>Wake, but to claim it's the only useful use for Wakes is tunnel
>vision.

There's an old saying from poker that one should "Only bluff once at a
sitting." It usually means get caught bluffing wildly early on in the
night, then never do it again, since you've put the idea in your
opponents' heads that you're lying, and from then on any time one of
them assumes you're lying he'll be (painfully) wrong. =)

>I usually put 1-5 Wakes in decks, depending on the deck. For intercept
>decks I usually put more, but I've found 1-4 Wakes to be extremely
>useful. Why? Because it keeps people on their toes. Once I demonstrate
>that I have Wakes, I can use it to bluff, tapping out and letting
>people think that I have a Wake when in fact I don't - or doing it
>only when I have a Wake, depending on how the game is going. You know,
>"mind games" and "strategy"? :) Being predictable is a bad thing.

That's excellent mind game, yeah. I even recommend it for other cards
- a deck based around Form of Mist shouldn't have many Forms of Mist
in it, since after seeing a couple your prey will suddenly quit
blocking you and if you've put too many in, assuming that your prey
WILL constantly block you, you'll have 7 Forms of Mist in your hand in
no time. =) You can conceivably get away with only playing a couple.
=)

The problem with bluffing based on Wake is that first, when you get
caught, it's not usually a "small" bad thing that happens. =)
second, ... in our group, usually you see Wake being played to untap
and defend against one's predator. consider this: if I am your
predator and you tap out your 3 vampires early on in the game, I will
look at you and evaluate your deck as best I can. Is it some form of
racing bleed that doesn't defend itself? Is it animalism untap? Is
it any sort of intercept deck? I will think "Hm. Well, he tapped
out. He probably has at least one Wake in hand. If he's bluffing,
we'll find out awfully quick." The problem is that a deck doesn't
make any progress v. Wake when it's sitting and defending. If I
decide "ok, he has a Wake, and I have no stealth in my hand", then I
can either waste time with my own vampires hunting, equipping stuff,
recruiting retainers, and basically doing lots of +1 stealth actions
that you may or may not bother to Wake for, and STILL may draw no
stealth into my hand, or I can just say "Well... either he has it or
he doesn't", and send 3 guys to bleed for 6 and see how many times you
untap. If you don't untap on the first, I may tap out to see if you
untap on the LAST or are just waiting for "zee Big One!" If i have an
obvious vampire who can play "zee Big One!", i'll try to do as much
damage as I can with the little ones first to draw out any Wake you
have. Perhaps even use up all my Conditionings on the little guys
with little Dominate, just because you're letting those through and
worrying about the guy with +1 bleed and big Dominate. =) Anyway...
why I don't like wasting time waiting is... what am I waiting for?
You'll never discard the Wake if you -did- in fact have it, because
you know you'll need it. If you didn't have it, you won't discard it
either, so there's never a signal to me that it's OK to come get you.
In fact, about the only thing that I can be sure of is that the more I
let you cycle cards without making you burn any, the more likely it is
that you HAVE drawn one and definitely aren't bluffing anymore. So I
might as well take actions against you and see if you have it NOW.
The only real thing it'll do is make me order my actions carefully to
see if you're inclined to Wake for one of the early ones, instead of
Wake for the steamroller that I absolutely WANT to get off. (And adds
an component to deck design - being sure of not being caught while
taking actions and/or not being damaged if you ARE caught. combat
defense; it isn't just for backwards anymore! ok sorry.)

Even bleed bounce is much more bluffable than Wake, since you can
always have it, and once you show it, your predator will constantly be
pondering "Ok, he didn't block. Do I modify it and potentially bleed
his prey for 6? Or do I leave it at 3 when he's maybe out of bounce?
If he lets a bleed for 3 go, is he just waiting for the bleed for 6 to
bounce it?" A true horror for any heavy-bleed deck =)

>In short: if you're basing a deck around the concept that it must
>always be able to Wake, then using N of them is a good idea. But I
>strongly disagree with the idea that that's the *only* way to use
>Wakes. Your mileage may vary, of course.

Mine has. =) but it may just be a difference in playgroup style. =)

Thanks for saying that straight out, Mark. I actually haven't played S&B in a
long time, mainly because I thought it was nasty & evil & degenerate at first.
I was the guy in our group who got trapped into trying to play intercept
combat, and usually getting my ass handed to me. But S&B is not scary under
NCL.

To illustrate, a month or two ago, I was playing a 4-player game, and my prey
was !Malkavian S&B. My deck would have shut him down just as quickly if *I*
had been the prey. I was playing my wacky Tremere Potence/Thaumaturgy rush
deck. My prey got out about 4 or 5 vampires, including Virgil & Vasantasena.
The *only* actions any of them had time to take were dragging themselves out
of torpor. Sabine Lafitte, Merill Molitor, and Sarah Cobbler *crushed* the
!Malks because they had no combat defense to compete with Immortal Grapple
followed up with Walk of Flame in the next round. S&B can be cowed easily
whether you are the predator or prey, and there are a number of effective
methods to do this in NCL, which Mark referred to, sort of. Intercept works,
but I think it's generally the weakest option. Blood gain, when it gets
rolling is better. Rush combat is next, and it's a favorite on the newsgroup
because it is *not* reactive...allowing you to use your vampires/resources to
maximum usefulness, hopefully. I think that bleed bounce is the *best* way
to shut down S&B. There are 4 (I think...?) bounce cards
available...Deflection, Redirection, Telepathic Misdirection, and My Enemy's
Enemy. In general, I think Deflection is preferred, because although it
costs 1, your vampires don't tap. Redirection is probably slightly better
than Telepathic in most decks, but if you're playing intercept/bounce,
Telepathic is the one to go with. Personally, I can think of less use for My
Enemy's Enemy, because you don't have a choice who it gets bounced to, but I
suppose in smaller games this will matter less. Now...only 2 groups of
vampires generally have access to all 4 of these, the Malkavians and the
Tremere. You really need 3 or 4 of these to have a *consistent* bleed bounce
defense in 4CL. In NCL, however, you can determine which is most appropriate
to your deck. Do you have big Ventrue with *lots* of blood on them? Go all
Deflection. Do you have lots of small Toreador with guns? Go with mainly My
Enemy's Enemy (that's +1 int at inferior, right?). I hope the picture is
clearer. Under 4CL, if you wanted to build a deck that could bounce most
bleeds that come at it, you need 2 disciplines that are only found in 2
clans. One of which you have almost ruled out of playing altogether. And
really, once the Tremere are bouncing, they've used up a significant portion
of their room for combat support.

> 4CL doesn't tame S&B at all. NCL makes it another deck, with probably
> a 1 in 5 chance of winning at a 5 person table, same as any other well
> constructed and well played strategy.

Very true. IMO, most well-built decks have a method of defense against most
counter-strategies. If you want simple, here's the defense strategies with
Nosferatu rush.

vs. S&B: Combat. Send minions to torpor/burn before they harm you.
vs. vote: Combat. Send minions that may vote to torpor. Send minions after
the prince who called the last harmful vote.
vs. prey: Combat. Make him keep spending more for minions.

There you have it.

How about a classic Ventrue vote deck?

vs. S&B: Deflections
vs. vote: counter-vote from permanants & cards from the hand.
vs. combat: Skin of Steel

LSJ> To strike, your fist (or other strike element) must traverse the
LSJ> distance from you to your opponent. When striking with First Strike,
LSJ> either your traverse that distance faster (e.g., Fast Hands) or
LSJ> you attack from a position/vantage point that allows your strike
LSJ> to connect before your opponent can connect his strike to you
LSJ> (e.g., Back Stab).

This would logically be because your reactions and speed are quicker.

LSJ> When Dodging, however, you are not attempting to get your strike
LSJ> from here to there. You are simply moving out of the way of the
LSJ> incoming strike.

If someone is trying to get out of the way of an attack that moves faster
than they are able to (Fast Hands) or an attack they don't know is coming
(Silence of Death) or an attack from a superior vantage point (Back Stab),
they are still unlikely to be successful in avoiding the strike. I don't see
why First Strike vs. Dodge doesn't take this into effect since Dodge is
_still_ just a strike.

If you don't believe me, try to dodge a bullet.

LSJ> When ending combat, the situation is much the same.

Not really. S:CE strikes are usually due to some pre-emptive power.

In the LARP, Majesty is an aura of immense charismatic power and
anyone within the range of the aura must try to overcome this aura
before being able to attack. Even if you have Super-Duper (tm)
Celerity and Quietus, you still have to overcome the aura first.

Most of the other S:CE cards are based on similar effects. Catatonic
Fear, Staredown, Eyes of the Serpent and Mercy for the Weak are
also based on extreme charismatic power and intimidation. Earth Meld,
Form of Mist, Mummify, Rapid Change and Shadow Body are based on
a pliant or insubstantial form. Spiritual Intervention and Preternatural
Evasion is based on foreknowledge of events. Riposte (a misspelling of
ripost...let's hear it for WotC editors) is based on a critical strike
(I suppsose).

LSJ> It doesn't mean "surprise attack" (see above).
LSJ> That's what Hidden Lurker mimics - and Hidden Lurker *does* thwart
LSJ> dodge and S:CE.

Blessing of Durga Syn (an illusion) and Silence of Death are both arguably
based on "surprise attack".

LSJ> Try using "real world" terms that work to convey the official
LSJ> operation. Certainly using terms like "surprise attack" when
LSJ> descibing First Strike can lead to confusion.

If you know the basis for the cards, I don't see how you could
argue that the 2 cards above aren't based on surprise attack.

LSJ> Not likely, since it isn't a problem (or, if it is a problem, it isn't
LSJ> severe enough to warrant such a change).

Depends on who you ask. Based on a close examination of the
cards, I'd argue that First Strike should be resolved before Dodge
but after S:CE

ber...@mich.com wrote:

> Can you give me an example of how allowing First Strke pre-empting
> a Dodge somehow puts Jyhad out of whack? It certainly would be a
> more well received rule change than some others..

Makes equipment even more generally worthless as stealing and
destroying become much easier?

Makes the Assamites too powerful? Not likely, but a possiblity. :)
More than likely, they would be brough on par with the other combat
oriented clans.

As it currently stands, First Strike only does you any good if the
other guys actually trying to hit you back rather than run away (S:CE)
or get out of the way (dodge).

Cards affected:

Backstab - Moves towards being really useful. Still requires a block.
Blessing of Durga Syn - Chimerstry steal with first strike
Canine Horde - If they are at long range with a weapon, they probably
already aren't going to dodge.
Fast Hands - Celerity steal with first strike
Muddled Vampire Hunter - Would improve slightly
Shattering Blow - Potence destroy with first strike
Silence of Death - First strike with hand or melee. Since Assamites are
generally better at long range, I don't see it helping them a ton.

And that's it. Are there any real benefits from changing how First
Strike works in the rule book? Not really other than possibly eliminating
some confusion. Perhaps the words First Strike should be chandged to
First Attack. Then you don't have any sensical problems. :)

Mike

Agree with your comments on the S:CE game world effects (i.e. an
attacker must overcome Majesty etc in order to attack), so on second
thought having S:CE beat First Strike is more-or-less logical. Also
agree with you that First Strike should beat dodge.

I know it's a minor point (like LSJ said), but it still *is* a
point. As a counterpoint to the "it's such a small thing that it's not
worth the bother to change it" argument, one could also say that
*since* it's such a small point, changing it would involve minor
effort and would make quite a few players happy. Change a few lines in
the rule book, issue a new Rules Team Ruling.

Essentially, it would make Muddles a bit more scary against weenie
decks (IMHO a good thing) and give Assamites and other clans with
celerity a weapon against dodge by using Silence of Death / Backstab
(IMHO also a good thing).

Personally, I *do* know that the "dodge beats First Strike" rule
causes a major "huh?" factor for new players. Having S:CE as the only
special class of strikes would help, IMHO.

//Petri

>
> LSJ> To strike, your fist (or other strike element) must traverse the
> LSJ> distance from you to your opponent. When striking with First Strike,
> LSJ> either your traverse that distance faster (e.g., Fast Hands) or
> LSJ> you attack from a position/vantage point that allows your strike
> LSJ> to connect before your opponent can connect his strike to you
> LSJ> (e.g., Back Stab).
>
> This would logically be because your reactions and speed are quicker.

Well, because your speed is quicker, yes. Celerity and all.

> LSJ> When Dodging, however, you are not attempting to get your strike
> LSJ> from here to there. You are simply moving out of the way of the
> LSJ> incoming strike.
>
> If someone is trying to get out of the way of an attack that moves faster
> than they are able to (Fast Hands)

The attack moves faster than they do, but they have to cover a
much shorter distance - the point of the attck. So even at their
"slower" speed, they can manage to get out of the way in time.

> or an attack they don't know is coming
> (Silence of Death) or an attack from a superior vantage point (Back Stab),
> they are still unlikely to be successful in avoiding the strike. I don't see
> why First Strike vs. Dodge doesn't take this into effect since Dodge is
> _still_ just a strike.

Right. Just a strike that protects the dodger from the opposing
strike, regardless of the opposing strike's speed. I still don't see
why the people who argue against this don't take this into account.

> If you don't believe me, try to dodge a bullet.

Improper argument. Try moving out of the way just as your
opponent attempts to pull the trigger. Much easier (esp.
for an immortal).

> LSJ> When ending combat, the situation is much the same.
>
> Not really. S:CE strikes are usually due to some pre-emptive power.

OK. So long as we both agree that S:CE should preclude First Strike.

> ripost...let's hear it for WotC editors) is based on a critical strike
> (I suppsose).

Riposte is the proper spelling, according to Webster' II New Riverside
University Dictionary.

And I have no idea how that (riposte) is supposed to produce a
combat ends effect. But there it is. :-)

> LSJ> It doesn't mean "surprise attack" (see above).
> LSJ> That's what Hidden Lurker mimics - and Hidden Lurker *does* thwart
> LSJ> dodge and S:CE.
>
> Blessing of Durga Syn (an illusion) and Silence of Death are both arguably
> based on "surprise attack".

For Silence of Death, sure. Durga Syn, not so much, but arguably so.
(It could just be a distracting tactic).

I suppose the card designers just used the First Strike effect to
simulate the surprise attack for Silence of Death, because attempting
to do so by other means (like Hidden Lurker) was considered too
complicated (or too powerful?). It seems like a Hidden-Lurker-style
effect would have been more appropriate for Silence of Death. As
it is, Silence of Death can give you a "surprise attack" on your
additional strikes in the round (oh, big surprise there) or even
on the second or later rounds. So the "surprise attack" explanation
still fails for the current implementation of Silence of Death.

> LSJ> Try using "real world" terms that work to convey the official
> LSJ> operation. Certainly using terms like "surprise attack" when
> LSJ> descibing First Strike can lead to confusion.
>
> If you know the basis for the cards, I don't see how you could
> argue that the 2 cards above aren't based on surprise attack.

OK. And the implementation could've modelled that better. But
(by opting to use the S:CE mechanic, among other things), it didn't.

> LSJ> Not likely, since it isn't a problem (or, if it is a problem, it isn't
> LSJ> severe enough to warrant such a change).
>

> Depends on who you ask. Based on a close examination of the

> cards, I'd argue that First Strike should be resolved before Dodge
> but after S:CE

Based on a close examination of the cards and rulebooks (throughout
the ages), I'd argue that First Strike is right the way it is
(and maybe some of the cards should've used a different mechanic,
but it's a little late for that now - and certainly no reason to
change the mechanic those cards use to match their particular
slant).

The "wack" 40% - 60% rule is not "in force" by the DCI - it is an
optional rule that individual tournament coordinators can choose

before the tournament. If it is not announced before the tourney,
then it is not in force. [DCI 2.1.1]

I call it an example of 4CL introducing degeneracy into the game.

ineffective.
In my experience, under NCL, S&B isn't cheesy. It's an exciting and
difficult deck to win with. There are so many viable defenses - bounce,
rush, intercept, race, or gain - that you have to have a good deck and

interest. I'm curious as to why some people want to make the game's
tournament rules more biased toward degeneracy.

Let's see if I can tackle this issue. Readers be warned. This post may
take a while and is likely to be about as intersting to read as Bills of
Congress from 1872.

To begin with, please note the fact that while the original VTES book does
say, "A "dodge"...prevents the effect of the opponent's strike that round,
even if the opponent's strike was delivered with First Strike," there was
no such statement in the Jyhad rulebook. And as has been pointed out in
the past, there were many problems in the translation from Jyhad to VTES.
However, both books do say, "The damage inflicted by a minion with First
Strike is resolved before the strike of the opposing minion begins," and
can be used as a basis to declare that First Strike _does_ happen before
S:CE and Dodges.

When I examined the cards that gave First Strike and Dodge, I examined
them based on effect and opportunity cost. The cost of opportunity can
be summed up by the following factors: Inf./Sup. Discipline Requirement,
Blood Cost, Restrictions of Usage, and Additional Benefits. I found that
the cost of opportunity of First Strike was much higher (almost 3 times
as much) than the cost of opportunity of Dodges. The fact that a Dodge
can cancel most of the strikes that you may get from a First Strike leads
me to believe that there is a serious game balance issue...esp. when you
consider that _any_ minion can use Dodge and very few minions can use
First Strike.

Restrictions of Usage includes the following: DNR (do not replace until
combat has ended), Equip (requires the opposing minion to have
equipment), Weapon (requires equipment to be a weapon), Close (must
be at close range), Blocking (must be blocking minion) and SL (Strike
Limit) (places additional limits on the type of strike the minion is
allowed).

Additional Benifits offset the cost of opporttunity and include: Press
(additional press) Strike (additional strike) and Steal (opponent gets
to keep stolen equipment). Destroying equipment was not included
because the pool loss from the burned equipment is often less than
the blood (and pool) loss from a damaged, torporized or burned minion.

The headers will be abbreviations for: Discipline (inf=1, sup=2), Blood
Cost, Restrictions (1 for every restriction on it use), Benefits (1 for
every additional effect), Total and Notes. The points from Benefits will

improvement from such a simple change (Of course, it sucks that
the relavent cards are Rare). The lack of variety in combat, and
the power of some of the trump cards has turned several people
I know off the game.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Dhar...@yahoo.com wrote:
> To begin with, please note the fact that while the original VTES book does
> say, "A "dodge"...prevents the effect of the opponent's strike that round,
> even if the opponent's strike was delivered with First Strike," there was
> no such statement in the Jyhad rulebook. And as has been pointed out in

The Jyhad rules state that the Dodge "negates the effect
of the opponent's strike that round" without making a special
exception for a strike done with First Strike.

> the past, there were many problems in the translation from Jyhad to VTES.

And that there were many ambiguities/errors in the Jyhad (as well as VTES)
rulebook. A valud explanation is that the (redundant) fact that Dodge
beats First Strike was simply omitted, intentionally or not.

> However, both books do say, "The damage inflicted by a minion with First
> Strike is resolved before the strike of the opposing minion begins," and
> can be used as a basis to declare that First Strike _does_ happen before
> S:CE and Dodges.

Except the S:CE explicitly states that it beats First Strike and
Dodge. And dodge explicitly states that it negates the effect of
the opponent's strike. Since it doesn't make any special provision
for not negating a First Strike, that can (and is) used as a basis
for the current rule.

> When I examined the cards that gave First Strike and Dodge, I examined
> them based on effect and opportunity cost. The cost of opportunity can
> be summed up by the following factors: Inf./Sup. Discipline Requirement,
> Blood Cost, Restrictions of Usage, and Additional Benefits. I found that
> the cost of opportunity of First Strike was much higher (almost 3 times
> as much) than the cost of opportunity of Dodges. The fact that a Dodge
> can cancel most of the strikes that you may get from a First Strike leads
> me to believe that there is a serious game balance issue...esp. when you
> consider that _any_ minion can use Dodge and very few minions can use
> First Strike.

Very nice evaluation [snipped], but the handling of the conclusion is
not so clear-cut.

The opportunity cost of the dodges should be less than the opportunity
cost of the First Strike. This is because of the difference between
defense and offense.

For instance, the opportunity cost of intercept is less than the
opportunity cost of stealth for this very reason. While some
cards have direct comparisons, LostInCrowds :: EnhancedSenses, there
are no equivalent comparisons for effects like Mr. Winthrop, a
Raven Spy, or KRCG News Radio. For instance, the closest thing to
Raven Spy (a non-unique retainer that requires a discpline) is
the Marijava Ghoul. The Ghoul costs an extra blood and is only good
on a specified discipline's actions (rather than requiring that
discipline in the first place - a more lenient restriction).

This is also why there is no direct antithesis for Ascendance.

And why Consanguinous Condemnation doesn't have the exact opposite
effect of Consanguinous Boon (indeed, it has a *much* lesser
effect).

does.

Why do you think that a dodge is "faster" than a normal attack, or even
an attack with FS?
Fact is: if a vampire is in combat with another one, and the first has
Celerity and the other hasn`t, then the cel-guy *is* faster using his
discipline. (In RPG terms, the cel-guy could perform x actions in a
combat round, where x is his celerity level (rather blood he spends),
the other one gets only 1 action.)
This means cel-guy can strike the other so fast, he cannot react in time.
This again means he cannot dodge in time, because defending is not
by any means faster then attacking.

In VTES terms: FS is mostly (with 2 or 3 exceptions) a cel ability.
(i.e. Fast hands, Backstab). FS can mean two differnt things:

1. the defender is too slow to react in time, so the strike hits, regardless
of the defenders strike response. (which could be even a dodge)

2. the defender is surprised (attacked from behind or whatever), and cannot
react in time, as he doesn't see the danger coming until it's too late.

In VTES, FS represents both! (Think of Fast Hands and Silence of Death)
FS is a concept, and there is no reason, why a minion should be able
to dodge a first strike. From a real-world view this is not right.

It would be different, if the dodger would dodge with first strike, too.
Then his dodge would again have effect against the FS.

>
> Some cards that perhaps are "surprise attacks" in concept (Noal
> mentioned Silence of Death) used (perhaps unwisely) the First
> Strike mechanic to implement the concept. FS doesn't do as good a
> job at modeling a "surprise attack" as Hidden Lurker's card text
> does.

Leave HL out of this discussion. It has nothing to do with FS. We
are confusing things here. HL is a special designed card, just for
VTES. It represents nothing in VTM-terms.

Because it resolves before a normal attack or even an attack with FS.

If you're looking for the "real world" explanation, allow me to
rephrase the point that I've made more than once in this thread:

It is easier to move the short distance from where the opposing strike
will land to where it won't than it is to cover the distance from where
your fist is to where your opponent's head is (or used to be).

distance = speed * time
time = distance / speed

Fist Strike increases the speed.
But the distance to be traversed by the dodger is much less
than the distance to be traversed by the striker. So the time
it takes the dodger to get out of the way is still less than
the time it takes the First Striker to complete his strike.

> Fact is: if a vampire is in combat with another one, and the first has
> Celerity and the other hasn`t, then the cel-guy *is* faster using his
> discipline. (In RPG terms, the cel-guy could perform x actions in a
> combat round, where x is his celerity level (rather blood he spends),
> the other one gets only 1 action.)
> This means cel-guy can strike the other so fast, he cannot react in time.
> This again means he cannot dodge in time, because defending is not
> by any means faster then attacking.

If you say so. I don't play the RPG.
The rules of the card game don't support that interpretation.
I'm sure there are many other examples of where the rules of
the card game do not match the rules of the RPG.

> In VTES terms: FS is mostly (with 2 or 3 exceptions) a cel ability.

> (i.e. Fast hands, Backstab). FS can mean two differnt things:
>

> 1. the defender is too slow to react in time, so the strike hits, regardless
> of the defenders strike response. (which could be even a dodge)
>
> 2. the defender is surprised (attacked from behind or whatever), and cannot
> react in time, as he doesn't see the danger coming until it's too late.

It actually means (only):

*. the attacker is moving faster than normal.

This doesn't mean the defender is too slow to react at all - but
that he is too slow to connect with his own strike against the
attacker, if that was his intention, until after his opponent's
strike connects. But the defender is still capable of moving. If
the defender chooses "dodge" as his move, then the amount of
movement required is so small that he is still successful in
getting out of the way by the time the attacker's strike reaches
the spot where its target used to be.

> In VTES, FS represents both! (Think of Fast Hands and Silence of Death)
> FS is a concept, and there is no reason, why a minion should be able
> to dodge a first strike. From a real-world view this is not right.

No. It represents speed only. Some cards have used it (First Strike)
to attempt to simulate a surprise attack. Some other cards used
a more appropriate mechanic to simulate a surprise attack (since First
Strike doesn't do a good job simulating a surprise attack - since
it wasn't designed to).

> It would be different, if the dodger would dodge with first strike, too.
> Then his dodge would again have effect against the FS.

So pretend that every dodge actually says "with First Strike" if
that'll help the rules make sense to you.

> > Some cards that perhaps are "surprise attacks" in concept (Noal
> > mentioned Silence of Death) used (perhaps unwisely) the First
> > Strike mechanic to implement the concept. FS doesn't do as good a
> > job at modeling a "surprise attack" as Hidden Lurker's card text
> > does.
>

> Leave HL out of this discussion. It has nothing to do with FS. We
> are confusing things here. HL is a special designed card, just for

> VTES. It represents nothing in VTM-terms.

HL was designed to simulate a surprise attack. It did not use the
First Strike mechanic to do so because the First Strike mechanic is
not suited for that sort of use.

First Strike is for speed, not surprise. Which is why Dodge "beats"
First Strike.

When the discussion involves the concept of surprise attack, Hidden
Lurker is appropriate for the discussion. (Psyche, on the other
hand, ...). If you'd like to leave HL out of the discussion, then
simply leave surprise attack out of the discussion - neither one
has anything to do with First Strike.

Messages.Author: Vince Johnson
Messages.Body:
>Fact is: if a vampire is in combat with another one, and the first has
>Celerity and the other hasn`t, then the cel-guy *is* faster using his
>discipline. (In RPG terms, the cel-guy could perform x actions in a
>combat round, where x is his celerity level (rather blood he spends),
>the other one gets only 1 action.)
>This means cel-guy can strike the other so fast, he cannot react in time.
>This again means he cannot dodge in time, because defending is not
>by any means faster then attacking.
>

You cannot use the RPG in this case because the rule of dodges *does* apply
in the WW system. Regardless of another character's celerity rating, you
can always dodge if you have the capability to and while unlikely, you can
outdodge a vampire with a rating of 5 in celerity (meaning 5+1 actions per
your one) in a single round without a single level of celerity. The other
thing to remember is that first strike is in no way connected to Celerity
anyway, looking at first strike cards will see that most don't rely on
celerity(m. vampire hunter for example).

Also dodge is described as taking the time to get out of the way of
another's action for the round. You're implying that even if combat range is
determined as close, that the 2 vampires are locked solid together in combat
when that isn't true(except in the case of IG which is a card combat action
for close combat). The difference is that despite the inability to move out
of range your vampire spent his time getting out of the strike of your
opponent, not running up to the other vampire, screaming in his face and
running away expecting not to get hit.

As for the response to long range combat and guns at any range, the
representation here is that your vampire found a very good place to dodge
behind to get out of the line of fire. This is the similar representation
in the RPG itself when at any range, the dodge becomes easier when in
cluttered areas where there are plenty of places to get behind. Your
playing of a dodge card of any type means your vampire was able to get to
cover instead of sticking around to fight.

S:CE is a different case, in the RPG relating to the case of Majesty, the
ability is consistently active(although the effectiveness is different at
different times and to different vampires). The game version prevents any
vampire from attacking unless they overcome the Majesty of the vampire. The
card game version is a representation of this in that the other particular
vampire is adversely affected by the majestied vampire, and thus would not
be able to have ever made an attack. The discipline cards in the card game
are representations of effective uses of their vampiric abilities. The
vampires ALWAYS have their abilites and can use them, but without them using
them effectively they don't add up to much(and would provide too powerful of
abilities, imagine if Majesty was permanent how powerful it would be).

Vince



Some cards exist which could've been written better, yes.
Some of them use the First Strike mechanic.
