None of them unbalance the game, so there is no compelling
reason to increase the errata list to alter the situation
(either by altering the rules or the cards themselves).

> > > It would be different, if the dodger would dodge with first strike, too.
> > > Then his dodge would again have effect against the FS.
> >
> > So pretend that every dodge actually says "with First Strike" if
> > that'll help the rules make sense to you.
>
> Why should I pretend that?

So that the rules (as they have always been) regarding Dodge and
First Strike will make sense to your conception of First Strike.

> Ok, for simplicity, lets say that there are only two speed levels:
> normal and fast. (As the game mechanic suggests)
>
> Strikes with fast speed resolve before strikes with normal speed.
> All strikes are at normal speed by default. (We leave S:CE out of
> the discussion, as we don't dispute them)

Also leave out Dodge (as the rules indicate).

The speed levels in question only apply to strikes that attempt
to connect to the opponent.

> So a dodge against a strike, both with normal speed, has effect.

No, it is at "dodge speed" - actually it is at normal speed but
has so little to do that the normal speed allows it to resolve
almost immediately (before a connect-with-the-opponent strike
done at either fast or normal speed).

> If both strikes are at fast speed, one is a dodge, the other a strike,
> dodge is effective.

True.

> If only the other strike is fast, and dodge normal, then the dodge would
> havne no effect.

No. The dodge (having so little to do) still resolves first.

If the point hasn't been made clearly enough already (which is
hard to believe), let me break down exactly what I mean in
physics terms (none of this is necessary - the explanations that
have been given and the rules themselves are clear enough):

D: Distance. S: Speed.

D (for punch) = X
D (for dodge) = Y (Y = X/4, e.g.)
S (normal) = N
S (fast) = F (F = 2N, e.g.)

Time to dodge = Y/N = X/4N
Time to punch = X/N ; Y/N = X/4N < X/N : dodge wins.
Time to punch with first strike = X/F = X/2N; Y/N = X/4N < X/2N : dodge wins

Of course, you can choose different ratios, even some that lead to
the conclusion that First Strike beats Dodge. But that would just
mean the ratios were inappropriate for the illustration, since Dodge
does beat First Strike (in a manner similar to the one illustrated
with the ratios above).

If that explanation doesn't clear it up for you, then just
take the rules at their word: Dodge beats First Strike.
Futher repetition of the points made would serve no purpose.

Does it also amaze you that no errata has been issued implementing
a Card Limit? People "largely" like card limits as much as they do
altering the rules on Dodge, as far as I can tell.

But, since both card limits and first-strike-beats-dodge do not match
the intention of the game nor do they promote game balance (criteria
for issuing errata, criteria which I thought you had agreed with in
the past), such errata is not issued.

If your group prefers to play with errata implementing a Card Limit
or with errata that changes the order of strike resolution, then use
that errata as a house rule. But unless the errata serves to correct
an unbalancing situation or restore the original intention of a rule
or card, that errata won't be issued. Even some errata that meets
one or both of the criteria mentioned doesn't get issued (when the
effect of the errata isn't great enough to warrant the change - like
Concealed Weapon).

I fail to see how applying a uniform guideline for issuing errata
after careful study of the issues can be seen as "dismissing it
out of hand".

Noal, I'm going to have to shoot you down now that I'm home. In the
LARP and table-top primary rulebooks (I don't have any supplements, so
it is possible that there might be an alternate rule that is akin to
First Strike), there is nothing like first strike.

In tabletop, Celerity gives you extra actions. In each turn, a vampire
with Celerity may spend one blood to get as many extra actions as they
have dots, or points, in Celerity. You don't get to do things before
other people, you just get to do more things.

In the LARP, you get abilities rather than dots. However, they also
only give you extra actions. Equal levels of Celerity cancel each
other out. Higher levels vs. lower levels adjust to the difference.

Alacrity - If you know a physical threat is coming, you can use this
to take a preemptive action. Examples given are drawing a gun of your
own, moving out of the path of a falling object, and so on. By this,
I take it to mean that you can't use it for a preemptive strike, or
what would be a First Strike.

The other Celerity abilities aren't even close.

Swiftness - You can make an immediate second attack after your current.

Rapidity - You can make two extra actions, otherwise like Swiftness.

Fleetness - Three extra actions.

First Strike is purely a CCG notion borrowing the term from Magic.
What it really should have been called was First Attack.

In tabletop, if you've still got dice, you can always try to roll a
dodge. You get dice to roll depending on your skills. (_very_ simplified)

In the LARP, you always get to try to dodge if you've got the actions.

This is all taken from "Laws of the Night," the LARP rules reference and
"Vampire: the Masquerade," the tabletop rulebook.

So now that the whole RPG/LARP argument has been shot down, can we move
on just spouting opinions back and forth rather than supposed fact? :)

Mike

important to fix (as they do not have a negative impact on the game as a
whole), and once you open the can of worms that is fixing weak cards, there is
a pretty long line of cards waiting to be fixed.

Messages.Author: Petri Wessman

Ok, since LSJ seems to be incapable of justifying the "Dodge beats
First Strike" rule except with "the rules say so", here's my take on
what "First Strike" means:

<tadaa>

A First Strike is a strike that happens before the other minion can
react to this. In game-world terms, this can either be because of
superior speed (Fast Hands), horde tactics (Dog Pack) or surprise
attack (Silence of Death).

In other words, there are multiple game-world reasons for the First
Strike effect. Celerity, surprise, etc. The effect (i.e. game
mechanic) remains the same.

//Petri

Messages.Author: Petri Wessman
Messages.Body:
Sigh.

Ok, to avoid quoting millions of postings, here are some condensed
opinions:

a) Circular logic isn't a useful argument, nor is repeating "it's in
the rules" when we are discussing the validity of those very same
rules. Especially when the subject in question *is not* in the
original game rules.

b) On the other hand, modeling everything after the RPG/LARP isn't
very useful either when we're talking about CCG rules.

c) People are talking about "minimizing the errata", and giving that
as a reason why an apperently popular change shouldn't be
made. Let's examine that argument for a second.

The current online rules document effectively doesn't matter. What
matters is the validity of the printed rules booklets and the total
resulting pile of errata. Now, the V:TES rulebook is essentially
the most useless (read: out-of-date) rule document at the moment,
since the massive LSJ changes have mostly been back towards the
Jyhad rules. So, the closest *printed* rules document that we have
are the original Jyhad rules.

Now, it turns out that those rules don't mention one way or the
other on the matter at hand. So no damage there. Also no change in
the complexity of the rules, in fact they would simplify a bit. No
additional "errata" is needed, just a withdrawal of a V:TES rule
interpretation.

So, on the plus side we have a change that would make the rules a
bit more comprehensible and give a small boost to a class of cards
(*not* just one card, note). The ONLY drawback I see is that it
requires a new version of the online rulebook and a Rules Team
Ruling to go with it.

Now, I fully understand the reluctance to change a card just to
make it useful, and if this was one card I wouldn't bother to
argue.

But: we're talking about a class of cards, with possible new cards
being issued by WotC in the future. IMHO, the benefits of doing
this now by far outweigh the disadvantages. I think we all want to
make this into the best game it can be. IMHO this is one (small)
step in that direction. Having the rules "make sense" is important,
especially when teaching the game to newbies.

It seems that the majority would be in favor of this change, going by
news/email messages and the opinion of the players we have here in
Finland. Of course, judging any sort of general player opionion is
more-or-less impossible - but this is an indication of *something*.

The reasons I've heard so far as to why NOT make the change are:

1) Too minor to be worth changing (DISAGREE, as I've outlined above).

2) Changes shouldn't be make just to make a card useful (AGREE in
general when we're talking about single cards, DiSAGREE in this
case).

3) Would result in yet more errata (mostly DISAGREE, see above).

4) LSJ thinks Dodges are always faster in game-world terms (DISAGREE
with LSJ's interpretation of what First Strike means, and think
making Dodges into a special case makes the rules unnecessarily
complicated).

5) LSJ says Dodges beat First Strike because the (V:TES and current)
rules say "Dodges beat First Strike". (DISAGREE, duh. "We can't
change the rules because the rules say so". Kafka would be proud :).

In short: I understand LSJ's reluctance in this matter, but don't
agree with the reasons he has put forth. At the very least, this
ruling should be taken into consideration the next time a Rules Team
Rulings document needs to be issued.

//Petri

I wouldn't be that harsh. I personally like most (not all) of the
current rulings, and understand that LSJ and the Rules Team cannot
please everybody.

However, in the current matter is looks like LSJ's personal opinion is
clouding matters. So far I can confidently talk about a "majority"
here, since I've kept track of the opinions. Something like 75-85% of
the people who have voiced an opinion on this matter think this
minor section of the rules should be changed.

Now, if someone could give me a reason why the change would be bad for
game play, I'll gladly shut up. So far I haven't heard one. On the
other hand, lots of people have commented on how it would slightly
improve game play, and make the rules more comprehensible.

What I *have* heard are rationalizations that amount to "it's too much
of a bother and I don't personally like the idea". This is not a valid
argument, at least to me. Anything that is beneficial to the game is
something that should be pursued IMHO.

slightly help balance game play - not much, but slightly. Now, each
RTR so far has contained changes that weren't absolutely necessary to
game play or balance, but which were "nice, small improvements". How
is this different? Until someone convinces me otherwise, the only
reason I see is that LSJ doesn't like this idea. With most people on
this newsgroup FOR the idea, this sets a nasty precedent unless
someone comes up with an explanation of why this change would be bad
for the game.

I'm listening.

> There is nothing about that in the rules. Drop that silly
> assumption! NOW! ;)

> >
> > True.
> >

> fighting class? Have you ever practised combat skills? NO?

Please offer concrete corrections.

> As said above, there may be times where you have little to do
> to dodge, but more often than not, it depends on relative speed
> (remember Einstein?) and the type of attack to be dodged.

?!

I *was* taking into account the relative speeds. I also was taking
into account the relative distances involved.

Einstein's Relativity has almost no bearing on the events in question.
Even Super Celerity doesn't begin to approach "relativistic speeds".

A "two trains" problem, while depending on the relative speeds of the
trains in question to one another, has nothing to do with Einstein's
relativity unless the trains are moving at large fractions of C
(to each other or to an observer in question).

> > If the point hasn't been made clearly enough already (which is
> > hard to believe), let me break down exactly what I mean in
> > physics terms (none of this is necessary - the explanations that
> > have been given and the rules themselves are clear enough):
> >
> > D: Distance. S: Speed.
> >
> > D (for punch) = X
> > D (for dodge) = Y (Y = X/4, e.g.)
> > S (normal) = N
> > S (fast) = F (F = 2N, e.g.)
> >
> > Time to dodge = Y/N = X/4N
> > Time to punch = X/N ; Y/N = X/4N < X/N : dodge wins.
> > Time to punch with first strike = X/F = X/2N; Y/N = X/4N < X/2N : dodge wins
>
> BAH. Mr Mathematician, you are X/4 and 2N are figures chosen by you.

As I said in the section you clipped. So?

> They by no means can be real. We don't know their speed. We only know
> that FS has a faster speed than normal strikes (Which would include
> dodge, as it is yet a strike).

The rules clearly indicate that FS is beaten by Dodge,so I chose
ratios to illustrate how that could be - ratios that showed dodge
moving at "normal" speed beating an aggressive strike moving at
"fast" speed.

The ratios were chosen for the express purpose of illustrating
the rules. As I said. And the ratios are not unreasonable.

As you say: We don't know their speed.
We only know that Dodge beats First Strike.

> > If that explanation doesn't clear it up for you, then just
> > take the rules at their word: Dodge beats First Strike.
> > Futher repetition of the points made would serve no purpose.
>
> Sigh. I know that the rules currently work the way you say.
> I would like to see that change. I merely argument for a change!

The arguments I've seen simply show how "First Strike beats Dodge"
is not unreasonable. Which I do not dispute.

They fail to show how "Dodge beats First Strike" is any of:

* contrary to (a possible) original intention
* unbalancing
* unreasonable
* worth the errata to change

"A rose by any other name would smell just as sweet."

The card could be called Janitorial Mishap. Net effect:

to the mechanics.

John Baker

Petri Wessman wrote:
> Which begs the question: who is on the current Jyhad Rules Team
> (besides LSJ)? What's the protocol that they follow? Who has how many
> votes? Why do we rarely see any discussion about new rule changes here
> on the Net before we're handed a Rules Team Ruling on that change?
>
> In other words, what is the group of people responsible for changes to
> this game, and where do they discuss things?

The Rules Team for VTES is composed of people who will remain
anonymous. The RT has members from different play groups
from a total of three continents. The protocol is discussion
and playtesting among the members of the playgroups and
reports of findings via e-mail. The topics for discussion are
suggested by the Net.Rep (me). Ideas for playtesting are
culled from the newsgroup (by me) and/or suggested by the
members of the RT. Members of the RT are also free to add
their own topics of discussion (well, not at first since
we had a full itenerary already, but once the initial fixes
were out of the way).

No one has any votes. Changes come by consensus.

The topics come from one or more of: the newsgroup/mailinglist,
private e-mail to me, or members of the RT. Mostly from the
newsgroup. The solutions may be "rarely" seen on the newsgroup
prior to the RT post, but the problems are almost always
brought up on the newsgroup prior to being discussed by the RT.

Similar, I think, to the way the RT functioned before June 1998,
except that the current RT relies on e-mail for communication,
has a wider base of members than the old RT, and has more members
than the old RT.

The whole business of the RT is not required by WotC. It's
just a concept I carried over because it seems like a good idea.

To WotC, there is simply an "ultimate rules authority" for VTES.
They leave the details of arriving at rulings/errata to my discretion.

<or...@termiitti.akumiitti.fi> wrote:

> Now, I fully understand the reluctance to change a card just to
> make it useful, and if this was one card I wouldn't bother to
> argue.

Really? It actually seems to only be two cards. Let's look at the
First Strike cards out there right now...

Muddled Vampire Hunter - ally, requires Malkavian
Canine Horde - Animalism, destroy equipment at range
Backstab - Celerity, only usable when blocking
Fast Hands - Celerity, steal weapon
Shattering Blow - Potence, destroy equipment
Silence of Death - Quietus, good for one round

Now... let's assume First Strike DID beat Dodge.

Muddles is a tiny bit more useful, but not much. His big problems are
still (a) having his Rush blocked by guys with 4 or more blood and (b)
S:CE. If it beat Dodge, he would certainly be quite the weeniebuster,
but that's a very narrow path of utility.

Canine Horde and Shattering Blow would be affected even less than
Muddles would - people with equipment are probably using the equipment
to protect themselves, not the Dodge. (ie. Leather Jacket as seen in
someone's weenie horde deck.)

Fast Hands wouldn't be affected at all. The only weapons our group
-ever- sees, except in "experimental toy" decks, are guns or a Sengir
Dagger maybe. If you have a gun, you're not doing "sideslip/blur",
you're using the maneuver to avoid damage and trying to shoot THREE
times. And you're certainly not disciplineless-dodging. As far as
Sengir Daggers, we don't commonly see those attached to Celerity decks
for some reason.

Backstab would be affected a little, since it's actually somewhat
likely that if you block someone they'll be using a Dodge to get out
of the way - but if I have Celerity, I don't need First Strike to beat
up on some guy who's relying on disciplineless Dodge. I just Blur and
pound him. Not to mention that Backstab qualifies as one of the more
worthless cards, IMO, for cost and circumstances - I can't see trying
to build an intercept deck around it figuring "sure, i'll equip an
ivory bow and use backstab with it to intercept my prey's actions and
send them to torpor!" ... Yuck.

Silence of Death would be the only card significantly affected by a
change in the First Strike rulings, since you can't exactly Blur when
using aggravated (taste of death) damage and may not have put very
many of those in your deck - the common Celerity counter to Dodge.

> But: we're talking about a class of cards, with possible new cards
> being issued by WotC in the future. IMHO, the benefits of doing
> this now by far outweigh the disadvantages. I think we all want to
> make this into the best game it can be. IMHO this is one (small)
> step in that direction. Having the rules "make sense" is important,
> especially when teaching the game to newbies.

The only -significant- benefit to be realized from altering the First
Strike rules would require that some sort of card be added to Celerity
to allow minions who AREN'T blocking to gain First Strike. Celerity
is a common enough discipline that such a card would effectively make
First Strike very much a part of the game again. THEN it could be
examined to see if First Strike really needed to beat Dodge or S:CE,
since it would actually have an impact on the game environment. (A
POT/CEL deck would become even more grim to face in combat, for
example.)

Want to fix Silence of Death? errata the card to, as someone else
said, be First Strike at inferior and "the opposing minion may select
no strike for his first strike this round" at superior. That -does-
make a lot more sense than altering the rules to effectively change
only one and a half cards.

i think i re-outlined this a little better above. agree IMO.

>2) Changes shouldn't be make just to make a card useful (AGREE in

it only really fixes Silence of Death - agree IMO

>3) Would result in yet more errata (mostly DISAGREE, see above).

Can't see this. it's one errata to the rulebook or one errata to the
Silence card. disagree IMO.

>4) LSJ thinks Dodges are always faster in game-world terms (DISAGREE
> with LSJ's interpretation of what First Strike means, and think
> making Dodges into a special case makes the rules unnecessarily
> complicated).

nah, this whole argument is because y'all are trying to relate it to
the real world, which is completely useless in this situation. =)
Throw this point out on BOTH yer parts and argue about the card game.
Yeesh. =) On a side note, yes, you CAN dodge faster than a strike
happens in the real world... Even if your opponent is an experienced
martial artist and you're not, you can always get out of the way of
the first one. You can't avoid the additional strikes he can cram
into the same flow of movement, though.... which also fits the game

>5) LSJ says Dodges beat First Strike because the (V:TES and current)
> rules say "Dodges beat First Strike". (DISAGREE, duh. "We can't
> change the rules because the rules say so". Kafka would be proud :).

Messages.Body:
"AgentZero" <agen...@my-dejanews.com> wrote:
> Now, I remember that the rulebook was quite clear about the
> Golden Rule of Card Ownership. However, you didn't find any
> problem changing that rule, a change which now has a *huge*
> impact on the game where before it was fairly neglible. This
> is but one indication of the inconsistancies in what you determine
> to be important enough to change. What? You got tired of
> stealing other players locations/vamps only to have them go
> away after they were ousted. Is that why you changed this rule?
> GRoCO had such a small part to play in the overall scheme of
> the game. Why are you so against the suggested change to
> FS when you had no problem changing the Golden Rule. At
> least the FS change will have a much smaller impact than the
> Golden Rule change had.

That was an example of change for the third reason changes are
made: simplicity/concept.

The old version of the GRoCO violated the concept of control, resulting
in in-game oddness. Similar to the oddness perceived by some members
of this newsgroup caused by the interaction of Dodge and First Strike.

Unlike that oddness, however, the oddness created by the old GRoCO
had *no* possible in-game concept or explanation to match the
rule itself. That, coupled with the fact that the new GRoCO is sligtly
simpler and not unbalancing, is why that errata passed review.

(Note the complete absence of any possible in-game concept as opposed
to the Dodge/First Strike problem where a *possible* in-game concept
exists to match the rule. Not everyone agrees that that concept, as
clear and simple as it is, is possible.).

--

> them ability to take out weenies without fear of dodges. In short, it
> would make them slightly better.

Backstab: Requires Celerity. Costs 2 blood. Gives First Strike for
one strike; at superior, you also get an additional strike.

Exactly how is this better for taking out dodging weenies than using
Blur: Requires Celerity, costs 1 blood, gives 1/2 additional strikes?

Silence of Death: Requires Quietus. Costs 1 blood. Gives FS for
remainder of round if you use hand or melee strikes. At superior you
also get a maneuver.

At least this one doesn't cost 2 blood. Still not better than Blur.
Can provide a maneuver to help with being at close for the hand or
melee action. However, being at long with Flash and using Taste of
Death has the same blood cost, and at superior you do have a press
if your victim Dodges. (And the Flash/Taste would send the victim
to torpor if they don't Dodge or prevent damage.)

> PDB6> It would open up a huge can of worms that is currently closed
> PDB6> (if you are going to fix First Strike cards, are you going to
> PDB6> fix Disguised Weapon? Chainsaw? Werewolf Pack? Hellhound?...)
>
> Those are single cards. This is a part of the rules. Very big
> difference. In addition, this requires NO card
> errata. Zero. Zip. Nada.

No, but it *is* a change to the rules, and one for a minor improvement
for all the cards involved except Muddles, who is *already* good even
without First Strike beating Dodge. And again, I don't think that
future First Strike cards would benefit that much from beating Dodge
either, because in the world of combat, Strike: Combat Ends is the
nine hundred pound gorilla, and if you can't deal with it, you just
plain suck.

Regarding the whole 'real world logic' thing, I'd just like to reiterate
that everything in the card game really is metaphorical and should not
be looked at too closely in 'real world' terms, because it will always
break down. Why does having Cats' Guidance let a vamp block more than
one action? Do the cats go out and get blood to keep him happy or
something? Why can people without Thaumaturgy use Wake With Evening's
Freshness? Why does a Saturday Night Special in the hands of some
random mortal always kill another mortal on the first shot?

In my view, Dodge shouldn't be looked at as physically dodging the
opponent's attack in very close quarters (as when sparring). If you
declare Dodge as your strike, it seems to me to reflect your vamp's
efforts to not be there when the other combatant tried to beat you up.
Maybe you hid around the corner. Maybe you were Behind Him! and snuck
off while he wasn't looking. Maybe you ducked behind a car when he shot
that .44 at you. Maybe you saw him ripping that Gate off its hinges
and made for the hills. Maybe you turned into Mist when you saw that
his Wrath was starting to Burn. Unless he's got you Immortally Grappled
or something, these are not unreasonable possibilities.

Josh

Messages.Body:
Petri wrote:
"Very small change, agreed, but still change, *especially* in the ease of
explaining the rules to new people."

I fail to see how saying "FS beats dodge" is any easier than saying "FS doesn't
beat dodge". What erroneous preconceptions people have about how something
should work based on their previous, unrelated knowledge has little bearing on
how a game should work. I play Titan. I used to play D+D. When I started
playing Titan, I didn't imediately assume that Trolls could regenerate in
Titan, just 'casue they could in D+D. Making Trolls in Titan regenerate
because they do in D+D is silly. Changing FS in Jyhad to work like it does in
another game is just as silly.

"Ummm... yes it would. Both Backstab and Silence of Death would give them
ability to take out weenies without fear of dodges. In short, it would make
them slightly better."

Slightly better in that they would have two extra cards that might be possibly
useful at their disposal, yes. However, to make an effective Assamite deck
currently, you need to be able to deal with S:CE, or your deck won't work. As
anything that can currently deal with S:CE can deal with Dodge, the Assamites
currently have no problem with Dodge. They can use Psyche, Additional Strikes,
and Pressess, all of which A) work perfectly well against dodge and B) fit into
a deck that can deal with S:CE. Removing some of these angles to include FS
cards as to be able to beat Dodge occasionally will do little more than
compromise the effectiveness of the Assamite deck.

"Those are single cards. This is a part of the rules. Very big
difference. In addition, this requires NO card errata. Zero. Zip. Nada."

Granted, but the reasoning is the same, and once you fix something because it
is too weak, you set a precident. If FS is changed, it would be done because
it is weak, not because it is too good. As has been pointed out before, it is
RT policy to only change things that are too good ("broken", "overpowered") to
make them more reasonable and consequently have less effect on the game
environment as a whole (cards or rules). It is not RT policy to improve things
that are weak so that they have more effect on the game environment as a whole.

Messages.Author: Xian
Messages.Body:
In article <79f831$qer$1...@oak.prod.itd.earthlink.net>,

"AgentZero" <agen...@my-dejanews.com> wrote:
> Now, I remember that the rulebook was quite clear about the
> Golden Rule of Card Ownership. However, you didn't find any
> problem changing that rule, a change which now has a *huge*
> impact on the game where before it was fairly neglible.

I'm inclined to disagree that it's a negligible effect. Prior to Ancient
Hearts, this was the case, but as far as I can tell, one of the biggest
reasons it was changed is because the rule as it stood, had a *huge* effect
on the Followers of Set. Assume you're playing a Corruption deck. You
primarily want to steal your prey's vampires. When you oust your prey, he
takes any vampires you've stolen with him. Net result: gain 6 pool, lose x
minions, many wasted actions.

In short, the Golden Rule of Card Ownership, unmodified, effectively
discouraged (almost disallowed) a whole game *strategy*. Changing First
Strike, while it would slightly (as I think Mike pointed out) improve combat
for some clans, is seen as not quite worthwhile, because it doesn't actively
hinder a specific strategy. Yes, it makes Assamites more likely to need to
resort to additional strikes, but hey...they were probably going to do that
anyway, right? And maybe a little more reliance on Psyche, but if you're not
using that in the first place, you're *asking* for pain.

In addition...(I'm not saying this is an argument in favor...I'm just
curious...) outside of JOL, are there really that many people who own enough
Silence of Death for it to make a difference? I have 1...I know there are
probably a number of people who have more...but how many more? I suppose it's
not like you're going to use Backstab in place of it, but still...

Xian

that are too weak for their cost looked at as well?"

It seems likely that they have been looked at. I am farily certain that it was
decided at some point, when the idea of errata was breached, that fixing weak
cards was just not worth it. In the name of keeping errata to a minimum, the
RT fixes cards that have a noticable negative impact on the game environment.
Cards that suck have zero impact on the game environment, as no one uses them,
and if they do, these cards don't compromise the balance of the game. Cards
that are too good, on the other hand, tend to dominate play and have a negative
effect on the game environment. Cards like ToRIII and RTI, for instance,
tended to completely warp a given environement (the competetive tournament
environment in particular) to the point of everyone being forced to either use
these specific cards or build decks to specifically deal with these specific
cards. Weak cards don't do this. They just get left out of decks. Thus,
fixing cards that are too good improves the game environment as a whole.
Fixing cards that suck just leads to tons and tons of extra, needless, errata.

"I know Concealed Weapon gets tossed in all the time, but to make
it a discipline-less card may make it too powerful and that
is clearly not the case in the First Strike vs. Dodge issue."

I'm iffy on the whole disciplineles CW issue. As to the FS vs Dodge issue,
personally, I really wouldn't care one way or the other if FS suddenly beat
dodge. I don't think it would improve the game (or be a particualr detriment,
either), I don't think it would have the effect that people hope it would, and
I simply don't think it is worth the effort, certainly if it means setting the
precident of "fixing things that suck".

I heartily dispute this point. Over 13 years in various martial arts,

primarily through well structured defensive tactics. It is far and
away easier to hold a speedy opponent at bay than it is to actually
launch a counterattack of any magnitude. If you compare the
expenditure of effort on the part of the attack to that of my own,

Bringing a game "into line" with the real world is a subjective thing
(as alluded to in the above counter "argument". We can all imagine
the counter response, and the counter-counter etc. ad infinitum.
Neither side could reach a mutually satisfactory conclusion. The
reason for that is because the applicability of the real world on a
CCG is restrained only by the two arguers imagination. That's the
reason why we all sound so foolish when we try these arguments.
They're word games, at best)
Bringing the game "into line" with the RPG is a questionable pursuit,
as it only benefits those players who find themselves playing the game
as a consequence of their involvement in the RPG. I don't know what
fraction of the world Jyhad population came to it from that route (I
was the opposite, CCG first, then RPG), but the idea that being more
like the RPG somehow makes the CCG better doesn't ring true to anyone
who doesn't come from that shpere. I'm sure that a CCG that mimics a
favorite RPG to a tee would be appealing to the people with that
hobby, but the rest of the planet could honestly care less. From the
standpoint of game design, to stick so close to the mechanics of the
RPG would be either suicide, as you automatically limit your
prospective customer base immensely, or competely aribrary. On this
ground, mimicing the RPG, while not to be explicitly avoided, should
not be a goal that drives change to the games mechanics.

As I think has been pointed out First Strike is not a suprise strike or fast
draw, merely one which resolves first. The suprise combat entry card which
renders your opponent unable to declare a strike is adequately covered by
other cards.

Dodge is a declaration on intent for that round, and works retroactively,
cancelling the effect of a strike. Even if you do not know from whence the
attack is coming you are performing, in the Star Trek parlance, evasive
manouvers. The original first strikes were used merely to remove weapons from
opponents hands Fast Hands et al., not to make a strike un-dogeable, and were
particularly amusing when the oponent had declared a strike with that targeted
weapon. The primary effect was to allow the strikes not to resolve
simultaneously, however dodge is 'retroactive', and it does not matter when i
resolves as long as it is during that (sub) round.

All that being said; the effect many wish to see in the game is already
reflected in suprise combat entry cards and as such we can suggest that the
intent of first strike (what was that myterious amulet?) was different to
these cards. First strike remains a useful, if not S:CE busting ability

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In article <79n0v2$49j$1...@nnrp1.dejanews.com>, CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at
writes

>I beg to differ. IMO the designers wanted FS to beat everything
>less than S:CE. As they did not include the sentence "beats even strikes
>dealt with FS", and the way strikes resolve are clear, it is perfectly
>understandable that it runs like this:

It is equally readable either way.

Whenever you get into situations like this, you have to work on some
things. For instance, when a card says something which is redundant
(reminder text) does that mean that a card without such a prohibition
doesn't suffer from that same restriction? e.g. Is the reminder text on
Telepathic Counter (V:TES) necessary? Would a card without that
reminder text still suffer from it, or would the requirement of it being
on Telepathic Counter mean that the lack of it over-ruled the rules?
(Golden Rule of Cards) Silly example, perhaps, but it happens.
Basically, in cases like this, brevity causes confusion where reminders
can be helpful, and that's the situation we're in now. Does the lack of
"reminder text" in the rules mean that Dodge should or shouldn't have
beaten First Strike since they can both be read as over-ruling the
other?

The original rulebook ruled that S:CE happened *now*, IIRC. First
Strike always beat normal strike, but not S:CE as I understand it.

The ambiguity comes in when Dodge says that it cancels the effect of the
opposing minions strike on this minion (hence not cancelling S:CE), but
does not reference the speed.

Does that lack of reference point either way? The lack of reference
*can* be taken as meaning that Dodge cancels the effects of the opposing
strike regardless of speed. Equally, it can be read as meaning that
First Strike gets in before it and so Dodge hasn't yet had a chance to
cancel that effect. However, given the fact that S:CE didn't have to
wait for resolution, it is eminently possible that Dodge didn't really
have to either. Again, though, it is possible the other way

If First Strike was intended to be a major part of the game, and a
normal speed dodge was intended to have been beaten by it, I would have
expected to see a foil such as:

Supernatural Speed
Celerity
Normal: Dodge
Superior: Dodge, with First Strike

The existence of such a card would, pretty much conclusively, have
indicated that a normal speed dodge was intended to be beaten by a first
strike, but then the superior would have beaten even a first strike.

We don't have such a card, so we don't have that guidance. BUT if First
Strike was intended to be a major part of the game, is it not
unreasonable to ask why, beyond S:CE, they did not include a specific
foil to it for dodges?

Again, though, we have only the rulesbook as "concrete" evidence, and
that can be read either way.

For my money, the limitedness of First Strike means that such a rules
change is unnecessary, really. Only, to my knowledge, Backstab and
Silence of Death allow you to activate it on your own (non-specific
strikes), and both of those pre-empt everything else (ie the choosing of
strikes), so you don't get the real impetus of thinking "Oh, but if I
dodge now, what happens if he plays First Strike? Shall I S:CE instead,
even though I would like to additional strike?" since it is in plain
view.

What, change for the sake of change? Stone is exactly what
rules are supposed to be made of. The Ten Commandments came
on stone tablets for a reason. ;-)

But seriously, the problem with changing FS as I see it is that
it would *still* be too weak even if it did beat Dodge. Dodge
is *already* a zillion times less good than Strike:Combat Ends.
Making it hosed by First Strike as well as everything else that
it loses to (but S:CE doesn't) serves no useful purpose. The only
benefit I can see is that, in the future, the designers might print
more cards with the words First Strike on them, thinking that they
would be good now. But in fact, they would most likely still suck.

did it... (they printed Backstab under the FS loses to Dodge rules,
hmm?)

FS was just a bad idea in the first place - all it was good against
under the original rules was people who tried to hit you with damaging
strikes, but who would go to torpor if you hit them first. Even if it
beat Dodge, it would not be that useful a part of the combat arms race,
because the existing FS cards wouldn't be much improved by beating
Dodge. And if they wanted to make new FS cards that would be good
enough to use, they would probably have to be overpowered compared to
existing non-FS cards (ie directly escalating the combat arms race,
probably in favor of celerity).

> Perhaps we should drop FS and additional strikes altogether,
> because, (if we can take it for granted) S:CE will always
> and ever be used solely. So there is no need to dodge, to FS,
> and to Additional. Now what?
> Easier game. K, but then I can also play M:TG.
>
> Sorry, I get a bit cynic nowadays.

That's all right, we're all cynics here. ;-)

One of the bigger problems for FS to overcome is that the obvious
discipline for it (celerity) already has plenty of other cards
that do what FS could do, only better. (additional strikes, presses,
combat restarting.) Making FS just a little bit better (beating
Dodges) simply isn't worth the paper you'd print the change on.

Josh

Oh yes, there is in fact one thing that S:CE loses to but Dodge
doesn't: Dog Pack.

> > strikes, but who would go to torpor if you hit them first. Even if it
> > beat Dodge, it would not be that useful a part of the combat arms race,
> > because the existing FS cards wouldn't be much improved by beating
> > Dodge.
>
> But improved nonetheless. The whole point was that changing it wouldn't
> make it so overpowered as to break the game. Minor change=Minor effect
> on game balance.

But the ones we have would still suck - the usual arguments I've seen
are that a more powerful First Strike would make it more likely that
we would see *future* cards using First Strike that would be usable.
I don't think there's any real point in doing that when the designers
could perfectly well just use card text to achieve whatever effect
they wanted.

To me, there is also a presumptive case against making any change that
makes cards more powerful rather than less, because it is worse for the
game to create overpowered cards than to make powerful cards less good.

> > And if they wanted to make new FS cards that would be good
> > enough to use, they would probably have to be overpowered compared to
> > existing non-FS cards (ie directly escalating the combat arms race,
> > probably in favor of celerity).
>
> Not true. Look at the FS cards we have now. Imagine that FS did
> beat dodge. Would any of those FS cards be overpowered compared
> to the existing non-FS cards?
> Nope.

No, that's not what I meant. The FS cards we have now, which suck,
(note inflammatory opinion) would still suck if FS did beat Dodge.
What I was trying to say was that, if designers tried to make future
FS cards that would be worthwhile compared to existing combat cards
for their disciplines, they would run a serious risk of escalating
the combat arms race.

> Call me mr. jade.

Sure thing, Mr. Jade. (Better than Mr. Pink.)

> Everyone keeps coming back to Celerity. Not all vamps/minions who
> have access to FS have access to Celerity (unless you put a Cel
> master on of course). Why restrict those who don't just because
> there are some that do?

The only non-Celerity First Strike cards I'm aware of are Muddles
(no disciplines involved), Canine Horde (ani), Shattering Blow (pot),
Blessing of Durga Syn (chi), Silence of Death (qui).

All of these except Silence of Death and Muddles are anti-equipment
strikes. The advantage of having First Strike on them is that it
'beats' the opponent trying to use the weapon on you. Having it also
beat the opponent Dodging to try and protect the equipment would be
gravy, but would have little impact on the overall utility of the
cards.

Silence of Death is in-clan only for the Assamites, who also have
Celerity. Muddles is a Malkavian card, works on his own, and is a
good card without First Strike being any better than it is.

I would be surprised if the designers created many more First Strike
cards outside of Celerity, because their card ideas do generally seem
to follow the role-playing game, and as far as I know (which isn't
far) First Strike is mostly a Celerity-related concept.

Josh

Wake/any +1 permanent intercept. Decks using +1 permanents, from what

cards to add to the intercept - so they can't necessarily afford to
burn blood for failing.

(intercept decks) If I just want to have a guy attempt to block
something while tapped, I'll use Wake. Especially if I'm going to
wakey-bouncey.

stop fixing overpowered cards -- I think it's pretty much been done

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Petri Wessman wrote:
> jhun...@dillinger-2.io.com (J. Hunter Johnson) said:

> > <CPilh...@bhak12.ac.at> wrote:
> >> Nope, LSJ started this by generally saying that a dodge is always
> >> faster than an attack. He did *not* say that in connection with the
> >> CCG, but on a more general basis. I simply did not agree with him.

I didn't start that. Indeed, I didn't even say that. Obviously,
even in the CCG, there are attacks that cannot be dodged. It's
just that "First Strike" isn't the thing that makes an attack
not-dodgeable (cf. Scorpion Sting).

Someone asked for an explanation.
Their assumption was that a standard First Strike could not be
dodged (despite the rules). They wanted an explanation (real-world)
of how that wasn't true. I gave them one. Which I had to repeat
many times in more and more belabored terms, eventually dropping
into (as someone called it) "pseudo-physics", even though the
concept is an extremely simple version of standard "two-trains"
problems.

Nonetheless, the example I gave was not that "dodge is always faster
than an attack". It is that dodge, even if it has a lower speed
than the speedy "First Strike" attack, executes in less time because
it has less to do.

> J> Wow, really? I would have sworn that I only saw that *in this
> J> newsgroup*, which is directly connected to the CCG. But then, I guess
> J> if you are compelled to cling to demonstrably incorrect mechanisms,
> J> you have to take your points where you can invent them.
>
> Whatever the newsgroup, if you make blanket statements then you have
> to be prepared to defend them. Don't imagine that the fact that this
> is a specific CCG newsgroup acts in any way as a filter. I for one
> understood one of LSJ's original arguments to be "you can always dodge
> an attack" (not in any CCG-specific context). This I disagreed
> with.

Misunderstanding.

I said that the "faster strikes" (modelled by First Strike) were
still not fast enough to connect to a dodger. You can always dodge
a dodgeable attack. Standard strikes, even when modified by
First Strike, are dodgeable attacks.

The types of attacks that cannot be dodged are modelled by Scorpion
Sting, Hidden Lurker, etc.

> On a martial arts / budo tangent, you can usually *block* an
> attack. That's different from dodging, which you can also do but which
> is much harder due to human reaction speed.

# New tangent. Note to people who would later claim otherwise:
# I didn't start this one, either.

So maybe "Dodge" in the CCG incorporates these kinds of
"real-world" concepts (block/dodge/misc. defense) into the
simpler term "Dodge".

The V:TES glossary simply defines "Dodge" as "A strike that cancels
an opposing minion's strike." That could well include concepts
like blocking and parrying.

(Like "bleed" incorporates many different concepts - to be applied
as "needed" to make sense.)

If it does or doesn't, no matter. Even if it is just a standard
english "dodge", it is still sufficient to avoid the damage of
a standard First Strike.

--

http://www.wizards.com/VTES/VTES_Rules.html

>Nonetheless, the example I gave was not that "dodge is always faster
>than an attack". It is that dodge, even if it has a lower speed
>than the speedy "First Strike" attack, executes in less time because
>it has less to do.

while the dodge, whether or not it has a lower speed than the speedy
"First Strike" attack, and whether or not it executes in less time because
it has less to do, still has to be able to "see" the strike coming in order
to dodge it... which is where I think the first strike thing comes in...

IMO (which is, I know, contrary to actual rulings) first strike should
beat dodge because the whole "english language" concept of a
first strike is a strike that happens first, before the opposing minion
would have a chance to dodge out of the way.... speeds have nothing
to do with it, it's timing... so I think that first strikes should resolve, than
S:CE, then everything else....

granted, it's not a major point, first strike would still pretty much bite..
but if you went up to some random people on the street who didn't
know this wonderful game of ours and asked them "if you have a
regular strike, it can be dodged... if you have a 'first strike', would
that be negated by the same dodge??", the obvious answer just
based on the concepts presented by the english language would
be "no, because it is a FIRST STRIKE"...

anyway...

No, I'm not.

You have expressed a desire to have an MJL presence on the Rules Team.
If you are given that presence on the rules team, by not following the
errata, you damage any credibility that team were to have.

Let us imagine a time in the future when another "7/7" is issued - very
controversial rulings based on, say, muck-ups in the new expansion
(hypothetically). If MJL had a presence in the Rules Team, would you
follow those rulings?

Again, if you don't, you would damage the credibility of the Rules Team.
You might not agree with the individual rulings, but to maintain
credibility, you would have to publicly support them.

Similarly if, now, you (being the MJL rep, rather than you, Noal) were
to sit on the Rules Team, not using the errata of that team would be
highly disrespectful and show contempt for a body you were attempting to
have influence over. And if you did change to using the rules, well,
why not change now?

I can't put it any simpler than that. If you wanted the place you
would, as I see it, have to use the Rules else there'd be no point.
You'd be creating official rules, and having a proper "say" in them, and
then just saying "Well, I don't like those crappy ones over there so
we're not using them, but you all have to use this one that I put
forward." To do that would be a snub to all those groups out there who
quite happily use 7/7 et al verbatim and who would carry on using the
official rules but who aren't part of the Rules Team even though, by
playing officially, they arguably have more "right" than an MJL player
would.

And, for the record, beyond LSJ, I know of no-one who is consulted by
the Rules Team. I have, on occasion, directly e-mailed LSJ with
thoughts on what appeared to be an imminent ruling (eg the reversal of
Strike: <something> Equipment) but beyond that, I have no direct
contact.

> Is there really extensive opposition to the modified Golden Rule?

In the MJL, yes. There is a huge resistance to changing the
printed rulebook, esp. in specific response to a particular strategy.
We didn't want to change the rules to benefit a "steal" stategy
and we didn't want to change the voting rules to prevent the
WVP strategy. We're still hashing out how we can make voting
balanced so that it doesn't overly benefit WVP or Presence
voting decks.

> of opposition. People get the impression that half the set has been
> rewritten, and express outrage accordingly. It has really been just a

*shrug* So where do you draw the line? We decided that certain cards
did need to be fixed (such as RtI) but felt that WotC errata was too
drastic. Instead, we came up with minor modifications to text that had
nearly the same effect as the WotC errata. Others we weren't convinced
needed to be changed, such as Mind Rape and WWEF.

> The problem stems from the fact that it was the overused, overpowered
> cards that were targetted, and people got upset to find that their decks,
> which naturally relied overmuch on these cards, no longer worked as well.

I was one of the loudest critics of the 7/7 rulings when it came out.
However, very few of my decks used any of the "overpowered" cards.

It was the trend towards completely changing the way the cards and rules
worked that got us upset. (i.e. 7/7 ToRIII errata, Mind Rape, Fame, RtI,
etc.) It was my belief that it set a bad precedent and I wanted new players
to be able to buy a few starters and boosters, put together a deck based on
the way the rules and cards were printed and be able to show up to a
tournament and play the deck.

Good Luck! If you wish to correct WVP, I seriously think, that accepting
the "no-vote-push" rule would be an important step towards the goal you
claim to strive for. This is arguably in line with the original Jyhad
rulebook, which was vague enough on the point.

As for Presence voting, I'm not sure how you intend to correct it. I'm
not sure it needs to be corrected, since Presence *should* be better at
voting than other disciplines. If you think the imbalance is too great,
then perhaps you could campaign for additional non-presence vote cards
being included in the soon-to-be-released mini-set.

> > That has always been a very popular house rule before it was made official,
> > and always met with unanymous agreement in my neck of the woods.
>
> Quite obviously, we live in different woods.
>

> > It makes a greater variety of strategies viable.
>
> No...it makes _one_ strategy more viable.

There are an limitless number of strategies, and how you classify them
into finite groupings is purely arbitrary. There are dozens of cards that
become more viable as a result of the new ruling. Each can be included in
an limitless variety of decks.

I am wondering what is this "one strategy" you are referring to. Do you
think that Settite Corruption decks are the only possible beneficiaries of
this rule? Here's a list of cards, many of them previously considered
marginal, that have received a boost: Lucian, Hostile Takeover, Malkavian
Time Auction, Succubus Club, Temptation of Greater Power, Amaranth,
Entrancement, Far Mastery, Fast Hands, Grave Robbing, Kine Dominance,
Disputed Territory, ...just from the first set.

> > I have also found, in my area, that the rewritten cards tend to meet alot
> > of opposition. People get the impression that half the set has been
> > rewritten, and express outrage accordingly. It has really been just a
> > handful of rewrites out of 1200 cards that work as printed.
>
> *shrug* So where do you draw the line?

I don't need to draw the line at all. That's LSJ's job. I don't, of
course, agree 100% with his rulings on all things. But one thing he has
definitely done is draw a line. Sometimes he, in my poor judgment, drawn
the line a bit too far, and in some cases not far enough... but he must
draw the line somewhere, and has in fact done that. It is clear that he
takes seriously the importance of issuing errata to cards and rulebooks
only when it is necessary (in his judgment, of course).

> We decided that certain cards
> did need to be fixed (such as RtI) but felt that WotC errata was too
> drastic.

Personally, I don't like complete rewrites either. In the case of RTI, I
would have preferred that it had been banned, though certainly something
had to be done about it. I doubt you'll come up with an appropriate fix.
When any card wins the game as an action, the cost becomes irrelevant. An
appropriate fix would have to involve preventing the card from directly
ousting, so that the cost (loss of a vampire) would create some risk or
disadvantage as far as gaining a victory point goes.

When you sacrifice an 11-capacity vampire to knock your opponent from 25
pool down to 9, then the cost is perhaps approptiate to the effect. The
problem is that the card is always used to directly oust, and you gain 6
pool and a victory point in the bargain.

> Instead, we came up with minor modifications to text that had
> nearly the same effect as the WotC errata. Others we weren't convinced
> needed to be changed, such as Mind Rape and WWEF.

It would appear that you are not opposed in principle to the idea that
errata can be necessary. You merely disagree with LSJ's judgment in
individual cases. These individual cases, however, are but a small
handfull of cards, out of 1200 printed. You could choose not to play with
these cards at all, and you would still have almost 1200 cards to choose
from, and an infinite number of strategies available to you.

I understand that the MJL maintains its own errata listing. Is is
significantly shorter than the official listing? Even if so, is the
confusion saved by having a slightly shorter list really worth the
confusion added by setting up a rival alternate list?

People get upset about fixes to overpowered cards mainly because they
see the cards too much. Nobody complains about the rewrite to Hidden
Lurker, because so few people play with the card that noone notices it
has was rewritten (long ago, by the old RT).

> > The problem stems from the fact that it was the overused, overpowered
> > cards that were targetted, and people got upset to find that their decks,
> > which naturally relied overmuch on these cards, no longer worked as well.
>
> I was one of the loudest critics of the 7/7 rulings when it came out.
> However, very few of my decks used any of the "overpowered" cards.

disproportionate extent, in the games that you play. Thus, you may have
an exaggerated perception of their importance to the game. Actually,
almost all of these cards could be banned outright without adversely
affecting the game, as you would still have almost 1200 cards to choose
from in designing your decks and crypts.

> It was the trend towards completely changing the way the cards and rules
> worked that got us upset. (i.e. 7/7 ToRIII errata, Mind Rape, Fame, RtI,
> etc.)

I believe you are incorrect in percieving this as a "trend". When LSJ was
given the authority, he insituted a number of changes that had probably
been long considered. From all indications, it appears he intends to be
quite conservative about any additional alterations. The latest errata on
TORIII is less radical than the first and puts the card more in line with
original text and card concept. He has resisted pressure to errata
Concealed Weapon and the First Strike concept. I see no "trend", and no
reason to make panicked howlings of "Where will it end!???".

> It was my belief that it set a bad precedent and I wanted new players
> to be able to buy a few starters and boosters, put together a deck based on
> the way the rules and cards were printed and be able to show up to a
> tournament and play the deck.

I agree that it is important to keep errata to a minimum for the above
reasons. I believe the vast majority of what is one the errata list is
(sadly) necessary, and can think of only a few instances where (IMHO) some
slight pruning of the list might be done.

Still, I believe the most confusion will come not from new players, but
from older players who know what all the "good" cards are, and put alot of
them in their decks. A new player will not play with so many of these
cards, and, unlike the experienced player, will not get the false
impression that most cards have been altered. The vast majority of cards
a Newbie plays with will work as printed (and will be more balanced in
power compared to the "good" cards an experienced player uses).

One example of how experience can warp ones perception is the (rather
funny) reaction of experienced players when you tell them that the damage
from Pulled Fangs is no longer aggravated. "That's crazy!" they howl, "If
it doesn't do aggravated damage then what's the point?" For years, these
players have seen this card burn vampires with ag damage every time it was
played, and so naturally assumed that burning vamps with ag damage was the
entire point of the card. A new player who read the text and title of the
card would assume that the point to pulling the vampires fangs to to make
it impossible to hunt (sending it into torpor if it must hunt and can't).
Experienced players are barely aware of this function of the card, because
it is completely irrelevant to a burned vampire.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Fri, 19 Feb 1999 Dhar...@yahoo.com wrote:

> My biggest problem with the 7/7 errata is that it gives a _HUGE_ edge
> to vote decks. Previously, clans that didn't use Presence could at least
> make a viable deck.

I think this is a good example of how experience playing with unbalanced
effects sharply limits ones awareness of available play options. There
are actually a whole host of cards and effects designed to assist with
voting. Most are ignored and dismissed as wallpaper. But wallpaper does
not exist in a vacuum. It is considered wallpaper because other cards
that achieve the same end are considered so much superior.

The problem is that the old PA cards were "broken" in the sense that they
turned almost all other vote modifiers and vote reactions into wallpaper.
Not only could they be used as action cards to call votes, but also as
vote modifiers to push votes and vote reactions to influence other
people's votes. Unlike regular vote reactions, you could play them even
if you had no untapped minions, and you could play multiples on a single
vote.

They were so good that they *almost* succeeded in eliminating from
competitive play two whole classes of cards: vote modifiers and vote
reactions. But not quite. The very best modifiers, such as the Presence
modifiers, were good enough that they were still considered worth putting
in a deck in place of yet more extra PAs, even though this usually meant
you were required to invest in somewhat higher capacity vampires.

A person playing in this environment would see only two tactics used: 1)
PA vote gain alone, which would tend to use weenies for greater
efficiency, since PA vote push needs no discipline, and 2) PA vote gain
combined with Presence vote modifiers, and using slightly larger
vampires. He might conclude that there are "basically" two types of vote
decks, "Vote Push" decks and "Presence Vote" decks (though actually the
Presence vote decks were also enhanced by Vote Push).

He might also conclude, based on simple Math, that if you take one of
these strategies away, then only one will remain, thus damaging game
variety. This perception, however, is false. When it comes to
unbalancing effects, 2 minus 1 could very well equal 20. A whole host of
vote modifiers and creative vote tactics will come creeping out of the
woodwork, which formerly never saw play since they just were not as
effective as a hand full of PAs.

To give one small example, I have definitely noticed, in the post 7/7
environment, the increased importance of the edge for getting votes
passed. Gaining the edge before calling a vote can make up to 2 votes
worth of difference in the count (one more for and one less against).
Night Moves (or some other stealth card) in a Nos Vote deck can be a
useful addition. In the Pre 7/7 environment, it usually made more sense to
replace the Night Moves with an extra PA or two. Same goes for other
tricky tactics like Cryptic Rider, or compromise politics, etc.

Since "no vote push" makes it harder even for "Presence" decks to push
votes through, all sorts of alternate tactics will be increasingly relied
upon. In particular large vampires with permanent votes will be have a
larger relative importance. Since large vampires typically have lots of
disciplines, this means that auspex and dominate vote cards are now more
likely to see play.

> Our current errata makes some effort to balance between giving the edge
> to Presence decks and WVP decks, but finding a perfect balance is
> probably impossible.

Before you try to correct the imbalance in favor of Presence voting, I
strongly suggest you try the current no-vote-push ruling on its own. You
may well find that no imbalance problem exists beyond what is approptiate.

A certain imbalance *is* appropriate since Presence was concieved as the
primary vote discipline. It is a fairly common discipline, posessed by 3
or the original 7 Camarilla clans, and by 6 of the 21 total clans. The
idea that you might need charm to succeed in politics is not so
inappropriate, though the Nosferatu still do pretty damn well.

Lupus Australis

So it takes just as long to explain all the errata, but 10 minutes
specifically to explain where your changes differ from the official rules?

From what I can tell from Noal's last posting of the MJL errata, these
are the changes:

Betrayer - is only slightly different, and no simpler than the WotC rulings
No mention if it totally replaces WotC errata or just what it directly
contradicts.
Ritual of the Bitter Rose - only diablerie
Aggravated Damage
Golden Rule of Card Ownership - States that cards are taken when the owner
is ousted. "Most alternatives riddled with holes ready for abuse."
What kind of abuse?
Beast - as written
Immortal Grapple - played as written on the V:tES version
Living Manse - States "Play as printed." Is this referring to the ruling
on 971204 that it must be burned before range?
Reform Body - Can be played by a vampire in Torpor
Return to Innocence - No action modifiers
Rutor's Hand - Played as printed, can have only one. This means that the
only way for the damage to be prevented at superior is with Blood Tears,
right?
Darius Styx - As printed (ie can target his controller?)
Fame - As printed, V:tES version
Mind Rape - As printed
Pulled Fangs - As printed but can only play one per round
WwEF - As printed
Zip Gun - As printed
Wooden Stake - As printed
Voting - DNR during vote. DNR PA's until end of turn
Sleeping Mind - "As printed" with the interpretation that Wake'd vampires
are still tapped even though they are acting as if untapped

And that's it. There are 11 cards or rules that are specifically played as
written, one that still often draws questions from players as to what they
do (Rutor's Hand - so how do I prevent the damage at superior?), and one
that has debatable interpretation (Sleeping Mind - Tapped vampires can
not block anyway, so how do the Wakes get around the rule and not get
around Sleeping Mind?).

Doesn't sound like the MJL minimizes errata at all when you consider there
are 106 errata and "corrections" when searching LSJ's web site.

From the official way, you can explain the 12 or 13 differences as follows.

Pulled Fangs damage is not aggravated. Immortal Grapple only lasts for
the round that it is played. Do not replace WwEF until your next untap
phase. Fame affects the vampire's controller. Ammo cards cannot be used
with Zip Gun. Beast cannot have or use equipment or retainers at all.
You can only use one political action card to gain a vote during a
political action, including any card that might have been used to call
the vote. Cards owned by a player that is ousted but are controlled by
someone else stay in play. Rutor's Hand does 3 unpreventable normal
damage rather than 1 aggravated damage at superior Thaumaturgy.

That leaves me 9 minutes to explain the other 5 or 6, some of which
could be left out of explanation or just noted as being different than
as written as they most likely won't be encountered (like Darius Styx
and Wooden Stake).

I do not see any "Great Simplification" like what David claims, because
otherwise, there is just as much errata as in the official rules.

No...Terror Frenzy has a cumulative effect, not a contradicting one since

combat cards. So...Dragos pays a base cost of zero blood, plus one blood
for each Terror Frenzy played. No contradicting effects that I can see.

> And "Acting minion" / "Acting player" isn't always applicable - take,
> for example, a Derange played on a Nosferatu who is Clan Impersonating
> a Lasombra. Is he a Lasombra when he takes an action, but a Malkavian

> Antitribu when the vampire who played Derange is acting?

Again this is an example of effects that are either cumulative or replace
previous ones. If Nosferatu plays a Clan Impersonation after being hit
with a Derange, he still changes clan, but the rest of the effects of
Derange remain in effect. If, in your example, the Nosferatu moves the
Derange to another vampire, I would expect that he returns to being a
Lasombra. Again...no direct contradictions there.

What it boils down to that the clause, "tapped minions may not blocK"
was obviously intended to prevent vampires from using WWEF and
Forced Awakening to block, otherwise the statement would be
completely redundant and extraneous. Note that it doesn't prevent
vampries from playing other reaction cards like Deflection and
Foul Blood. I may be inclined to believe that the effect _may_ be
too powerful for its cost, but the intent of the card is quite clear
and I'd have to see that it has a severe game unbalancing effect
before being convinced that current WotC errata is best for the
game.

On Mon, 22 Feb 1999 Dhar...@yahoo.com wrote:

> > Immortal Grapple - played as written on the V:tES version
>

> ...and Sabbat. Of the three versions, two state explicitly that hand strikes
> last all combat and the Jyhad version doesn't directly contradict this.

I'm curious to know if you are aware of the reasons for the official
errata on this card. LSJ will correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe it
was fixed more for reasons of "correctness" than balance.

The Jyhad version was clearly intended to work for one round only. The
superior version keeps the combat at short range for the second round,
creating an opportunity to continue the effect by playing another immortal
grapple.

The V:tES version has the odd effect of allowing situations where, if
combat lasts to a second or third round, the participants can maneuver to
long range and still only be able to do hand strikes due to the Grapple.
Boy, that's some strange grapple!

> > Rutor's Hand - Played as printed, can have only one. This means that the
> > only way for the damage to be prevented at superior is with Blood Tears,
> > right?

> Correct. If the option to prevent the damage with Tears was still open,

> I may have voted to go with WotC errata. But since it wasn't, I didn't.

I actually have a bit of sympathy for this one. If the RT were to remove
the errata on Rutors Hand and simply add a clarification that only Blood
Tears can currently prevent the damage, I would prefer it to the current
rewrite.

> > Darius Styx - As printed (ie can target his controller?)
>

> No...we're sticking to the original definition of (D) actions and thusly,
> there was no need to change the text. A (D) action can only target someone
> else.

The current approach is the original approach. The purpose of the (D)
symbol is clearly explained in the rulebook. It does not have anything to
do with who can or cannot be targetted.

The rulebook makes it fairly clear that the purpose of the (D) symbol is
as a sort of reminder text. The "Rampage" text makes it clear that the
symbol was not intended to restrict actions to opposing Methuselahs only,
and the definition of "directed action" makes it crystal clear that an
action which targets oneself is not directed.
